- FANNY OF THE Trill. There is a maid, whose lovely charms Are blo,ming in the sunny south, I joy to clasp within my arms, And taste the sweetness of her mouth ; And though she is of lowly birth, I've tried by every art to win This fattest nymph that tripe the earth— Delightful Fanny of the Inn! Her home's upon a sea-girt isle, Reposing near a lofty down, That o'er it sheds a pleasant smile, But seaward oasts an angry frown; Whose steep the tourist e'icebs to view The sun his daily course begin, But whither I ,epair to woo My radiant Fanny of the Inn And where I often hear her voice Uplitted in melodious song, That bids the peasant's heart rejoice, And brings around a childish throng ; And where at eve, when Fiddler Joe Disconrseson hie violin, I list the dulcet notes that flow Frem tuneful Fanny of the Inn! I've whispered in her tilted ear The fervent longings of my breast, And now the happy morn is near When she'll lull my bold request; For graciously she bath replied, And promised t.. be more than kin; And may each lover love his bride Al 11l love Fanny of the lont fiewl
J.H.L.

WHAT WAS HIS CREED? He left a ton of anthracite In front of a poor widow's door, 'When the deep snow, frozen and white, Wrapped street and square, mountain and moor. That was his deed; He did it well. , "What was his creed?" I cannot tell. Blest" in his basket and his store," In sitting down and rising up, , When more he got he gave the more, Withholding not the crust and cup. lie took the lead. In each good task— "What was his creed ?" I did not ask. His charity was like the snow, Soft, white, and silken in its fall; Not like the noisy winds that blow From shivering trees the leaves, a pall For flower and weed Drooping below. "What was his creed ?" The poor may know. • He had great faith in loaves of bread ' For hungry people, young and old; And hope-inspiring words he said To him he sheltered from the cold; For man must \ feed As well as pray. • "What was his creed?" I cannot say. In words he did not put his trust; In faith his words were never writ; He loved to share his cup and crust With any one who needed it. . In time of need A friend was he— " What was his creed ?" He told not me.

He put his trust in heaven, and worked Ever along with hand and head; And what he gave in charity Sweetened his sleep and daily bread. By word and deed To help the poor— That was his creed; What would ye more?
—Leeds Weekly Mercury.

-----.- "What are you thinking, my man? said Lord Hill to a soldier leaning in a gloomy mood upon his firelock after the battle of Salamanca. "I was thinking, my lord," said the man, "how many widows and orphans I have this day made for one shilling." He had fired 600 rounds of ball that day." Counsel for the defence: "That my client was driven to commit the offence Prom sheer necessity is plainly seen in the fact that he only took the trifling amount a cash which was in the drawer, whilst leaving untouched the pocket-book silh notes to the value of 2,000 marks which was lying close by." Judge: "Prisoner at the bar . . But what are you crying for?" Prisoner (sobbing): "Because I didn't see the pocket-book !" • EFesers OF' ALccaroL ON LONCIEVITY.—The effects of alcohol upon longevity is most decidedly injurious, In intemperate persons the mortality between 21 and 30 years of age is five times as great, and between 30 and 40 years of age four times as great as that of the temperate. It beornes gradually less -with advancing years, but at every age the abstainer has the advantage. An Intemperate Persoa's A Temperate Person's chance of living is— cloance;of living Is— At 20-15.6 years At 20-44.2 years. „ 30-13.8 „ „ 30-36.5 „ 40-11-6 „ „ 40-28.8 „ „ „ „ 50-21.25 „ • „ 60— 8.9 „ „ 60-14-285 , VENTILATION AND APFETITE.—In a weaving-mill near Manchester, where the ventilation was bad, the pro- prietor caused a fan to be mounted. The consequence soon became apparent in a curious manner. The opera- tives, little remarkabte for olfactory refinement, instead of thanking their employer for his attention to their comfort and health, madea formal complaint that the . -ventilator had increased their appetites, and therefore entitled them to a corresponding increase of wages. By stopping the fan a part ot the day, the ventilation and voracity of the establishment were brought to a medium standard, and the complaints ceased. The operatives' wages would but just support them; any additional de- mand by their stomachs could only be answered by draughts upon their backs, which were by no means in a condition to answer them.—Cassell's "Household

Guide." Here's a pretty tale of domestic economy, says Vanity Fair. He had been brought up in the lap of luxury and extravagance, and, when the bad times came, and he had to go down tp the City and look carefully after his shillings, it was his pretty and tender little wife who helped him and encouraged him by example in small savings. One fence, however, he never would face. He balked at taking a 'bus. "It might pass the club, you know, dear, and the fellows at the windows—" One evening, however, he returned radiant to dinner. Ten- derly embracing his life's partner, he murmured, "I've done it, darling! All the way for threepence !" Love and gratitude were in her eyes as she said, "My own brave boy! Did you mind it very much ?" With affec- tionate cheeriness he made answer," No, dear (Sot box- seat; real good old sort, the driver; told me lots of stories and good things for the Lincolnshire. Capital chap! Gave him a big cigar and half-a-crown for him- self when I got down I" MARRIAGE BY SURPRISE.—Many years ago an excel- lent Quaker gentleman of Philadelphia took to himself a wife without any formal ceremony, both the parties to the union believing a ceremony to be unnecessary. The Governor of the State, who was a warm personal friend of both, begged them to be married in due form, to which they objected, saying that they were married al- ready. But ene'day, the Governor, being invited with other friends to dine with the Quaker, adroitly turned the conversation upon the subject of matrimony. In the discussion which followed he addressed his host per- sonally, saying, "Seth, I understand thee to say that thou dost consider Hannah to be thy lawful wife ?" "Yea, verily do I," said he. "Thou wilt certainly cherish her as thy wife so long as thou shalt live ?I' "Indeed I shall," replied the host, looking proudly- at Hannah. Presently the Governor turned to the wife: "Hannah," said be, "thou dost love Seth as thy true and faithful husband 2" "Truly I do," said she. "And thou wilt always be a true and faithful wife to him ?" "Yea," said she. "Then," said the Governor, rising with dignity, "By thp authority vested in me as chief Salagistrate of this colimonwealth, ',pronounce you man sod wife." 'rum CHANNEL IsrstsMs.—Like the Isle of Man, in the Itish Sea, the Channel Islands are nearly independent of Great Britain, to which they owe merely a feudal allegi- allee: and while one of them has a Legislature and laws Of its own, the other three are governed together. The Legislature consists in each case of a "Royal Court," composed of the chief justice or bailiff, and twelve jurats; these officials, with twelve rectors, twelve con- stables, and fourteen deputies, form the Parliament. The bailiff presides, and he has the casting vote; but the Parliament sannot be assembled without the consent of the Lieutenant-Governor, a vice-regent appointed and supported by the British Crown, who also has the right of veto, though he seldom exercises it. The bailiff and rectors are appointed by the Crown for life, and the jurats are elected for life by the ratepayers. They are not required to have legal qualifications, but a butcher, a baker, or an innkeeper is ineligible. The Channel :Islands are the oldest possessions of the present ruling house of Great Britain, having passed to the English Crown through William the Conqueror. When Nor- n2aTtdy was regained by France, the islands chose to re- man with England, and, though Jersey had been at- ' tacked and invaded by the French, the population has maained loyal to E ng and—a fact the more remarkable since the language used is that of France. The words, "Fromt_he fury of the Normans, good Lord deliver us!" were added to the Litany, and the stoutest resistance made to all attacks. A good action is, never forgotten—by an attorney. Never owe more than you can pay, and nev‘r allow anyone to owe you more than you can afford tOgoise. If a man could be conscious of all that is said or him in his absence, he would probably become a very modest man indeed. . A market girl sold a gentleman a fine fat goose, war- ranting it to be young. It turned out, when roasted, to be unmanageably tough. The next day the gentleman said to the market girl, "That goose which you sold me for a young one was very old.' "Certainly not," said the girl; "don't you call me young ?" "Yes." "Well, I am but nineteen, .and I have heard mother say often that that goose was six weeks younger than me.' A two-foot rule was given to a labourer in a Clyde boat-yard to measure an iron plate. The labourer not being well up in the use of the rule, after spending con-` siderable time, returned. "Noo, Mick," asked the plater, "what size is the plate?" "Well," replied Mick, with a grin of satisfaction, "it's the length of your rule, and two thumbs over, with this piece o' brick and the breadth o' my hand, and my arm from here to there,

bar a finger. - TICKETS FOR ONE.—A rustic bridegroom met his bride on the station platform at Troy, and bought a ticket for Chicago by way of Albany and Susquehanna. When the train was made up the affectionate pair seated them- selves in the rear of the car and began to drink beer and make merry. When the conductor came along, the groom handed him the Chicago ticket, whereupon this dialogue ensued :—Conductor "Where is your other ticket ?" Groom: "Why, I ain't only got one." Con- ductor: "Well, is this lady with you?" Groom "Why, yea, of course she is." Conductor: "Well, when is her ticket?" Groom: "Why, Mr. Conductor, she is 'l4 wife. Don't you know, why, we just got married; my wife, don't you see; we don't need but one ticket." The con- ductor could not make the bewildered groom understand the rules of the road, and that it would require two tickets to carry them to Chicago, and finally when the train reached Schenevus the bridal party were put off. They took the next train to Albany in search of the man who had sold the ticket that was not good for man and .wife. TAME OrrEns.—Otters are quite capable of domestica- tion, and may be taught to catch fish for their masters. or this purpose they must be caught young, and gra- dually brought to live upon bread and milk. When this end is attained, they are taught to fetch and carry, like a dog—first sticks, &c., then a stuffed fish, then a dead one. When this part of their education is perfect, and they make no attempt to mangle the fish given to them, they are sent Into the water to catch living fish. Otters are trained for this purpose in India, and also in China, where they are used by the fishermen of the Yang-tse- kiang. Mr. J. Thomson says :—" We noticed men fish- ing with trained otters in this part of the river. There were a number of boats, and each boat was furnished with an otter tied to a cord. The animal was thrust into the water, and remained there until it had caught a fish; then it was hauled up, and the fisherman, placing his foot upon its tail, stamped 'vigorously until it had dropped its finny prey!' There- is one peculiar habit of the Canadian otter which is worthy of mention. "Their favourite sport is sliding, and for this purpose in winter the highest ridge of snow is selected, to the top of which the otters scramble when, lying on the belly, with the fore-feet backwards, they give themselves an impulse with their hind legs, and swiftly glide head foremost down the declivity, sometimes for the distance of twenty yards. This sport they continue apparently with the keenest enjoyment until fatigue or hunger induces them to desist."—Cassell's Natural History. ROYAL REVENGE.—The citizens of Alexandria erected as a monument to the Emperor Diocletian the bronze image of a certain horse, to which, indeed, they owed much gratitude. One Achilleus had set himself up as emperor in opposition to Diocletian. The Alexandnans took up his cause, and Diocletian had to besiege the city for eight months before it surrendered. Achilleus was killed, and the emperor ordered that as many of the citizens should be massacred as would bring the blood up to his horse's knees. The butchery began, and he went towards the place of execution; suddenly his horse stumbled over a body and fell on his knees, that were wetted with blood. The emperor's threat was fulfilled, and the horse deserved the gratitude of the citizens, for far worse had befallen them some time previously. Cara- calla, roused to anger by some jests and epigrams of the satirists of the great city—which had received him joy- fully and worthily,—fell upon the elders at a banquet, and on the youth of the city at the gymnasium, and had them all killed. The massacre and plundering lasted for several days; the waters in the harbour gleamed'red with the blood of the slaughtered citizens, and the num- ber of the killed was so enormous that the emperor dared not render any account to the Senate; in his report he boasted that he had spent these days in pious offices, and had sacrificed the men with beasts to the gods. Ile had a strong wall, with forts at intervals, erected all across the city, to reduce the inhabitants to unresisting sub- TiliSSion.—"Egypt,Descriptive, Historical, and Picturesque." THE Cumnie OF THE CELTS.—There are no sound data for accepting the popular belief that the Britons when Cwsar lauded were barely one remove from savagedom. Compared with the cultured Romans, they were unquestionably barbarous, but their barbarism was tempered by a certain culture which had been operating on the people for hundreds of years before the arrival of the Latin legions. The country was well peopled, full of houses; brass and gold money was used, and iron rings of a certain weight were employed in barter. The men of Kent, being nearest to Gaul, and therefore accustomed to mingle with their Continental neighbours, were in most respects the equal of the Gauls in civilisation. In the interior the majority of the people were ignorant or neglectful of tillage, living on the flesh and milk of their cattle, and clothing themselves in their skins, as did the people on the other side of the Channel. Their social obaervances were rude, and, if we are to believe Ciesar, the marriage rite was of the most primi- tive description, something very like a community of wives prevailing in certain regions at least. In battle they were courageous. They , could manceuvre with cavalry, and constructed a kind of chariot, which did such terrible execution among the invaders that Ciesar ex- pressly remarks, "Our heavy-armed legions were no match for such an enemy." Indeed, so fierce and obsti- nate were the Britons, that, had their capacity for union and tribal cohesion been equal to their bravery and energy, they might easily have annihilated the Romans. But in those days, as ever since, the Celt was entirely deficient in the power of uniting for a common end. Every petty chief insisted on being his ownlmaster, and fighting for his own hand. The result was that, attack- ing the common enemy singly, they were defeated piecemeal by a disciplined force, every portion of which acted in unison, as if it had been a machine. This is the accountof Tacitus, who tells us that in the time of Agricola, nearly one hundred and forty years after Ciesar's invasion, the Britons, though conquered, were not disheartened; "they were reduced to obedience, though not to bondage." Ciesar was master of the sea- shore only, and though his successors—Roman, Saxon, Dane, and Norman—gradually reduced the tribes in the other parts of the island, it is within but recent times that the Celts of Northern Scotland can be said to have fully submitted to the rule of any master except their own tribal chiefs—From n "The Peoples of the World" for June.

CHOOSING A WtrE.—The character of the late Dictator Barrios is illustrated by the manner in which he obtained his wife. A Guatelma correspondent of the Ontario Globe tells the following story :—Being on a journey into the interior, he was entertained by a merchant of some note, who had a daughter, a rosebud of a girl, whose beauty struck a responsive chord in the heart of the widower president. Before leaving the place he informed his host that he desired to make the girl his wife, but as she was not quite old enough to be married he wished her sent to school, and educated in English and French conversation, in music, embroidery, and painting. In about two years he thought she would be of sufficient age and accomplishments to preside in the presidential palace, when he would formally ask the honour of her hand in marriage. This proposition rather staggered the country merchant, and he was only able to reply— " Si, senior, the girl is yours ;" but in his mind he de- termined that no daughter of his should ever be the wife of Rufino Barrios. The president, however, kept an eye on the family, and twice sent an official to remind them about the school arrangements before the father carried it out. He also adv,rtised exten- sively that he had selected the maiden as his future wife, and would marry her as soon as her education was completed. The two years ' passed, and Barrios claimed his bride. The girl refused to marry him, and the father sustained her in the refusal, expressing his views of his would-be son-in-law in no guarded terms. To speak evil of the King is treason here, as it used to be in England in the time of Henry VIII., and the country merchant was promptly arrested. His pro- perty was confiscated for the. use of his Government, and le was sent to work in the street with a ball and chain on his leg. It sounds like a fifteenth century romance, but everyone in Guatemala knows the story is true. Finally, the girl, frightened at her father's distress, gave in, and begged the old gentleman to yield his con- sent. He reluctantly did so, and attended the most bril- liant wedding feast that was ever known in Central America. The bride received a diamond necklace and a coronet, half a million dollars in money, and the finest residence in Guatemala. The father was released from arrest, his property was restored to him, he was estab- lished in the banking business, and became the fiscal agent of the Government, which is worth a fortune to him every year. Barrios very generously forgave the old man, and the two are now great chums. Mrs. Barrios is the loveliest woman in Guatemala, beautiful in cha- racter as well as in person, socially brilliant and grace- ful, charitable beyond all precedent in a country where the poor are usually permitted to take care of them- selves, generous and hospitable, a good mother to a fine family of children, and a devoted wife, loyal to all the President's ambitions; and an enthusiastic supporter of all his schemes.

At the half-yearly rent audit of the Romney Mark estates of Sir Edward C. Dering, Bart., the tenants were again allowed a remission of 20 per cent of their rentals. An Ayrshire farmer, who has just retired, says he has been obliged to give up his farm, with great improve- ments, like many hundreds more, and that an Arbitra- tion Board is much required on the land question. Some cattle have been poisoned at Wagstaff Farm, Biddenden, Kent, from eating the young withered shoots from newly-fallen oak timber. Accidents from this cause are more frequent than many suppose, and great care is always needed to keep cattle away from the danger. Another cargo of South Australian grapes has arrived in London, together with a sample box of pears. The latter were in particularly fine,,oondition, and it is confi- dently expected that, in the wholeiale market, they will realise 6d. each. The retail prices for large pears at the present moment range as high as is. 6d. each. Dinar FARMERS AND Low PRICRS.—The Dutch farmers are reported to be in as great a stiait as any in Great Britain. The value of their dairy products has fallen so low that :no adequate remission of their enormous rents can be made. In some districts the rent seems gone. Prime quality Gouda cheeses are now delivered in Lon- don at 355: per cwt. I An exciting occurrence recently took place at Old I Aberdeen. As a funeral procession was passing along a narrow thoroughfare, an infuriated bull, which was being led in an opposite direction, attacked the horses of the hearse, one of the animals being severely gored. A scene of considerable confusion followed, and the funeral party had to scamper off in all directions for safety. One of the mourners narrowly escaped being knocked down by the bull, which ultimately was secured. Osx AND Asn in North Radnorshire are now out, but not in full leaf yet. The ash is rather before the oak, but very little. In South Montgomeryshire, on the other side of the water-shed, where the rivers run into the Severn instead of the Wye, the oak is rather before the ash, and there, too, they, are scarcely yet iq leaf to-day (June 12th). I conclude we are not likely to have either a very wet or a very dry summer, but an average.—G. A. H.—The oak is decidedly before the ash in North Lancashire.—R. , THE Ammucsx WHEAT CROP.—The June estimate of the American wheat crop, published by the Washington Department of Agriculture, represents the crop as wow than any grown since the Department first issued re- ports. The percentage is 62 only, against 70 for May, and hundred for a full crop. The estimates for Spring wheat, Only just out of the ground, cannot be worth much, but it appears as 97 per cent. The expected pro- duce of the whole wheat crop of the United States is put at 360,000,000 bushels, against over 500,000,000 bushels last year. CALVES SUCKING EACH OTHER.—Question: How to pre- vent calves sucking each other ?—Answer : Take any old bit of leather or worn-out harness long enough to go round the calf's nose. The ends may be joined by two or three iron or tin tacks, and let it have the same ar- ticles driven through it. Then, all that is required to keep this arrangement about half-way between the eyes and nose of the calf is a length of tape or webbing for putting at the back of the ears which may be nailed on the belt in the same way. When a calf that has ac- quired this habit pursues it, the calf that it would suck would be pricked, and, adcordingly, as it is sometimes termed, he would "skedaddle." That is enough. IRENT RenucTioNS.—At the half-yearly rent audit for the Romney Marsh estate of Sir Edward C. Deiing, Bart., the whole of the tenants received a discount of 20 per cent. The fine farm of Mains of Fordoun, on Lord Arbuthnott's estate' has just been let to Mr. M`Kenzie, SlaMs, near Ellon, at a rental of 255. per acre. The rent paid by Mr. Brand, the late tenant, was about 325. per , acre. The farm of Wester Ulston, on the Hartrigge , estate, the property of Lord Stratheilen and Campbell, , lately tenanted by Mr. Steadman, has been let to Mr. , Andrew Ormston, late of Clerklands, at a reduction of , 34 per cent. In consideration of the depressed state of , agriculture, Mr. Samuel Jas. Brown, of Knaresborough, has returned to his tenants at Horton-in-Ribblesdale, near Settle, 20 per cent, of their rents, and Mr. T. T. S. Metcalfe has made a similar allowance to his tenants in Wensleydale. Mr. Walter Morrison, of Malham Tarn, has reduced his rents 20 per cent. for the next five years. WORKING DAIRY AT THE ESSE'X SHOW.—Under the auspices of the British Dairy Farmers' Association, there was a dairy stand at the above show, where the pro- cesses of butter making on the most improved methods were shown. The Dairy Supply Company supplied the implements and utensils required, including a Laval's cream separator, which was worked at intervals by a Hindley's 2-horse power engine. Over 100 gallons of milk were put through each day, and the sweet cream , made into butter by Mrs. Holmes and her daughter, from I Bromley, Kent, both of whom were prize winners at the last dairy show. The working of the separator and the washing of the butter in the churn (before it formed into lumps) were processes of great interest to the onlookers. Mr. Primrose M‘Connell, Ongar, gave short explanatory lectures at intervals, pointing out that it was possible to , milk a cow, extract the cream, and make into butter in L less than an hour, sweet cream making the best, and that , it is essential to separate the buttermilk from the butter thoroughly, this being done by washing when in the churn while the butter is still in the form of small grains. The separated skim milk and butter found a ready sale. The principle upon which the sale was effected was that a 141 b. stone of live weight repre- sents an 81b. (Smithfield) stone of carcase weight. TRACKING A CALF TO DRINK.—Those who have had the mournful experience know that there is nothing more trying to the temper than the operation of teaching a young calf to drink. The process is familiar to every man who has brought up a calf from infancy. You seize a pail of warm milk, go into the stable, catch the calf by the ears, back him into a corner, and bestride his neck. The idiot rather likes this, and while you are reaching for the pail he employs his time by slobbering the lower corners of your jacket. You discover what the blockhead is about, and box his ears. You cannot help it. You feel that way, and let him have it. But the calf cannot tell for the life of him why he has been struck, and he gives a sudden and unexpected "flounce." He believes he will go and stay on the other side of the stable, but he does not announce this beforehand. He starts on -the impulse of the moment, and you cannot tell just when he arrives there. You ride along with him a little way. But the laws of gravitation are always about the same. Your legs one on each side of the critter, keep up with the calf for about a second, but your body does not. You slide over the calf, and your. back kisses the floor. Your head is soaking in the pail of milk. When you get up you are mad—uncommonly so. Milk runs from your hair, and imprecations out of your mouth, and you solemnly declare that you will teach that calf to drink or break his neck. The calf does not know of this resolve, and he glares at you in a stupid fright across the stable. He was not aware that he was the cause of your downfall, and wonders ignorantly what is the matter. You do not tryto explain it to him, but furiously catch him by the ears, look back over your shoulder at the milk pail, and back up towards it, dragging the calf after you. The calf is out of wind, and you have not a particle of grace left in your heart. You are astride of the calf's neck, and jamming the fingers of one hand in his mouth, you place the other on the back of his head and shove his nose into the pail, fully resolved to strangle him if he does not drink. The calf holds perfectly still—ominously so—and there is silence for the space of half a minute, at the end of which time the blockhead, who has not drunk a drop, suddenly makes a splurge, knocks the, pail over; you are again I reduced to g horizontal from a perpendicular, and when you rise the excitement is intense. You have been soaked with milk, "slobbered" on, and hurt. Not a drop of milk has gone down the brute's throat, and there he stands glaring at you, ready to furnish you with another free ride wherever you want to go. With an affidavit you seize the enipty pail, and hobble out of the pen, fully resolved to let the four-footed fool starve; and thus endeth the first lesson.—A gricature.

THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY., JUNE 27, 1885.
COTTAGE GARDENING

The warm weather of the past week has given an ina- 1 petus to all plants that have• been well established, but • has had quite a contrary effect on young seedlings that have not penetrated deeply into the soil as well as newly planted subjects. Of the latter, we might say that more have come to grief than remain to furnish our gardens. Plants received from a distance suffer immensely in this way; the majority being dead when they come to hand, and the, remainder are- sure to meet with disaster if planted in the ordinary way. When plants come to hand during such weather as the past week, they should Ibe immersed in water for a short time or till they show signs of reviving, when they may be taken out and placed in the soil either in small handfuls or pricked out Isingly moderately close, so that they will not give so much trouble to shade while they remain in that posi- tion. Immediately there is a favourable change in the ; weather they should be moved to their permanent quar- ters, where with care and attention they will soon estab- I lislhemselves. _ , _ _

BROAD BEANS are best stopped when they show flower; that is, the point of the shoot is pinched by the action of the finger and thumb. This disposes them to form pods much earlier than when permitted to grow their full length. The plants are also made steadier by the opera- tion, and consequently better able to stand upright. If there is a disposition to lean on to either side from the action of wind or any other cause, it is best to insert a few stakes on either side, and run a string along, giving it a turn round each stake. Celery is apt to bolt" if allowed to get dry at any period of its growth,'and it should have a soaking twice a week during hot, dry weather, and plants pricked out in beds for late plant- ing must be constantly watched as to water. THE FRONT GARDEN.—Roses that have been budded

or grafted on a foreign stock frequently throw up growths termed suckers. They are really produced by the stock, but might be mistaken for the rose itself in some instances. When our common briar is the stock, and that a standard or a dwarf, it is impossible to mis- take it. Suckers, whatever the stock that produces Ithem may be, are robbers of that which should go to feed the rose, and tUey must consequently be moved, and in order to do thifl effectually it is best to trace each one home and not cut it at the surface of the ground, as this only causes it to throw up two or three.more shoots Green fly is sure to be present on the flower buds and the tips of the shoots during dry weather or in the absence of heavy showers to wash them off and keep them checked. It is, however, rarely that the rose becomes free of the fly after it has once got a footing, unless some insecticide is applied, and we wish for nothing better than soft soap and tobacco water, and how to prepare them we have detailed more than once. The rose maggot is as industrious as ever, rolling up the leaves as well as bracing them together with its web. Happily, hundreds of these may be destroyed in a few hours by the simple process of squeezing the leaves between the finger and thumb, when the mortal remains of the grub will ooze out somewhere if he is there, which is not always the case, as the insect, after having per- forated to its satisfaction those leaves in which it has temporarily enveloped itself leaves them to perform similar operations on others. If, however, all curled leaves are operated upon with the finger and thumb, every grub will be destroyed. We learn from a pnvate correspondent that Mr. Willis (cashier to the London and North-Western Rail- -4 way at Lancaster) has a splendid specimen of Marechal , Niel rose in his greenhouse which has yielded hundreds of flowers this season. Our correspondent counted 120 on it about a fortnight ago, their colour and size, we are told, being unusually fine. THE WlNDOW:—Pelargoniums, before they expand their flowers, should be fumigated, as the operation can- not be conducted afterwards without destroying all flowers that may be open. It is safer to give two or three moderate fumigations than one strong one. If manure water or any liquid stimulant has been applied it should be withheld where the plants are about to open their flowers, as it affects the colour as well as causing the petals to drop prematurely. Fuchsias should be stopped every two or three nodes till about eight or nine weeks previous to the time they are required to be at their best, and the plants must not be allowed to exhaust themselves by allowing them to carry flowers till about three weeks before they are required.

A cruel joke at the expense of those iadies who are perpetually striving to gain a hearing in the Press has been going the round of literary circles to the effect that "they look much better in muslin than in print." Some thieves met a man, and, after robbing him, bound him and laid him under a hedge; they presently also met another man, whom they also bound and laid on the other side of the hedge. The first presently exclaimed, with a heart-rending "Oh ! I'm undone, I'm undone !" upon which the other bawled out, and desired that he would come and undo him also.

"AS I WENT SAILING." By THOMAS GIBBONS. Author of Boxing the Compass," "Naval Songs and Song Writers,"" the Way to Ichang," No. I.—OLD TRUES AND NEW IN THE FAR EAST. "Look ye! Master Traveller, unless ye note something worth seeing, and come home wiser than ye went, I wouldn't give a stag's horn for all your travels."—Old Ply. . _ _

is customary for contented dwellers in the West, untravelled citizens "who live at home at ease," to pro- nounce strongly against John Chinaman, and to regard his native land as a 'Twit°, outlandish, and pagan country, "where the compass points south instead of north 4 where men wear petticoats and women wear trousers; where they shave the head instead of the 'chin; where shoes, umbrellas, and lanterns are made, Of paper; where wooden anchors are used for ships; where etiquette commands people to put on the hat instead of to take it off; where they wnte with a paint brtish instead of a pen; where they pray to devils much more earnestly than to gods; where rank and title, instead of being hereditary, are retrospective, and ascend to a man's great grandmother, kc., instead of descending to his successors; and in fact where everything is grotesque, upside down, and entirely opposed to Western civilisa- tion." Yet China is a land of manifold attractions; and we gain instruction from the wide disparity between the manners of the Chinese and the customs of other nations. We find in China la civilisation that is unique, inasmuch as it is unlike any other social system of ancient or modern times. It is a land of wealth and organsa- tion teeming with a law-abiding population, whose habits industry, industry, economy, and loyalty will compare favourably with those of any country in the world. , Is 'China civilisation original? We regard the question with interest, and not without great speculation, remora, bering that the country as a whole remains in much the same condition as it did two thousaald years ago. The antiquity of Chinese institutions is so impressive, viewed at every point, that we become accustomed to regard a young Chinese as an antediluvian man renewed! China, for centuries, has been swarming with human life, capable of great works, yet it has run the same course, through those immemorial tracts of time, refusing to acknowledge any influence or power outside its own vast limits. Progress has marked the pathway of otlier nations almost beyond human conception, but the im- port of the word is scarcely understood in China, and certainly cannot apply to any part of the country un- touched by foreign contact, meaning thereby that we cannot trace advancement as a result of the natural outgrowth of the Chinese naind. China and Japan are so often named together—perhaps on account of their proximity—that a large proportion of home readers regard the conditions of the two countries as identical. But such in reality is not the case. While Japan has stepped to the front within twenty years, building universities and manning fleets of ironclads, and has opened lier ports for intercourse ,with the world, it is a ,reverse picture in the case of China. Even in the settle- ments devoted to foreign commerce, surrounded by every national diversity that people of the. West can carry to Eastern shores, the Chinese put up the barrier of exclu- siveness, eat their rice and burn their prayers, in a mariner peculiar to their ancestors in the days of Confucius. As we have said, the manners and customs of the I Chinese remain almost untouched by outside influence, for we cannot regard the foreign-built towns scattered along the coast as reflections of a progressive stage of Chinese opinion. Rather should we view them as the memories of a belligerent introduction to China, and as evidence of the wish of the Chines themselves to remain an isolated nation. Since the visit of a certain Captain Weddell, of the East India Company, in 1637, who drove out the Chinese and hoisted the English flag over, the Bogue Forts, in the Canton river, the roar of the cannon has been the pioneer of every attempt to introduce the trade and civilisation of the western ocean men" into China. Very naturally, under such circumstances, the Chinese have viewed all our advances with distrust, and and yielded only to superior military prestige, from time to time, when China has been called upon to open her harbours and her wealth to the merchants of the West. It is customary for readers personally unacquainted with the country to regard the settlements as essentially Chinese in appearance, where the traveller is supposed to find—

... Mandarins with yellow buttons, handing you conserves of snails; Smart young men about Canton in nankeen tights and peacock tails, With many rare end dreadful dainties, kitten cutlets, puppy pies; Bird's-nest soup which (so convenient!) every bush around supplies. But the picture awaiting us is a very different one ! Many of the open ports, otherwise and more correctly styled foreign settlements, contain splendid buildings, the hongs of the foreign merchants, grand residences, and altogether- present an appearance decidedly European. The Chinese have witnessed the strange spectacle of foreign-built towns uprising from their soil, yet have re- mained singularly passive, and in their social relations have kept themselves inviolable the while. We have found much that is interesting in the history of the foreign settlements, curious items which cluster round memories of rough and dangerous times in the Far East. Hong Kong , a: Ifourishing English colony, Canton, Ningpo, and Tientsin all possess an instructive history • but a glance at Macao, Amoy, and Shanghai, three of the oldest ' and, probably best known open ports in China, will suffice for the present. Macao is the oldest foreign settlement in China. I rw Nearly four centuries o the intrepid Vasco di Gama was waving the flag of Portugal in the van of maritime discovery. • The Portuguese, the Spaniards, and the Hol- landers were the early voyagers to the Eastern seas, and traces yet remain of these indomitable travellers. They took possession of many islands of the Eastern Archi- pelago, and established settlements. The Portuguese es- tablished themselves at Macao about the year 1737, and in time the settlement became One -of the most flourish- ing marts in the Eastern world. They also formed settlements at Ningpo, and other places to the north- wards. But the rapacious policy of the strangers, in their trade wifh the Chinese along the coast, led to many disputes, and ultimately the Portuguese were driven from Ningpo. The same conduct compelled them to re- tire from other places and strongly influenced the Chinese against them. The several embassies of the Portuguese to the Chinese, between 1517 and 1753, met with little success, and often presented a most humilia- ting spectacle. From the advent of the Dutch, and later of the English, in China the power of the Portuguese be- came diminished, and China, a century and a half it has been gradually waning, until we find of that influence the faintest shadows only in the Macao of to-day. Macao lies about forty miles from Hong Kong, on the west side of the estuary of the Canton river. The climate is accounted the most salubrious in South- Eastern Asia; the temperature rarely falls below 60 de- grees, and the sea breezes sweep over the island. The Portuguese settlement is situated .on the south-east side of Hiang-Shang. Long ago, doubtless, Macao was sur- rounded by the sea, and formed a small rocky islet of itself, about eight miles in circumference. The Chinese built a wall across the isthmus, and stationed a few troops there to prevent foreigners penetrating into the i interior of Hiang-shang. The town s very picturesque, rising in terraces on the acclivities of the hills, and a fine marine parade extends round the harbour. Old-fashioned fortifications crown the hills and command the points looking seaward. The aspect of the place, especially from the harbour, the churches and convents, the pubhc offices and barracks, all remind us of Europe. Many buildings are of the style of the 16th century; and while wandering through the narrow winding streets the venerable features of the place become more apparent and distinct. Altogether it is a pleasant spot, and full of interest to the curious rambler. At one time we can readily believe that Macao presented a very imposing appearance; but the town is a very ghost of its former importance, without commerce, and fast-decreasing revenue. During the first Anglo-Chinese war, when foreign merchants were compelled to withdraw from Canton, the city of Macao was the place of refuge, and during subsequent hostilities, notably in 1856, the fami- lies of foreign residents were removed to Macao and Hong Kong. i There s a curious description of Macao, translated from one of the Chinese provincial histories, perhaps two hundred years agot which is certainly worth repro- ducing :—" In the district of Heang-shan-kien, and at a distance of about one hundred lee from the city of that name, there is a promontory which runs out into the sea, and is connected with the mainland by a narrow istlinlus only, as the leaf of the water lily is supported by its stalk. The town is built upon this promontory, and is wholly inhabited by strangers without any Chinese at all amongst them; but at the barrier a cus- tom house is established for the examination of all per-• sons and goods that pass to and fro. The soil produces neither rice, salt, nor vegetables, all of which are sent to them from the interior. Within the town a European officer presides, with a rank similar to that of our gover- nors of provinces. All the government (meaning China) edicts and communications are explained to.them through the medium of an interpreter. One of their peculiar cus- toms is to salute by taking of the hat. We receive from them in trade the articles of ilry, amber, coarse and fine woollen cloths, red wool, sandal wood, pepper and glass." However accurate the Chinese historian may have been, writing two hundred years ago, as applied' to the Macao of to-day the description is certainly in- correct. The proportion of the Chinese population is now estimated at about six to one of foreigners, the latter being mostly of Portuguese descent. Nor is the , soil barren. It produces rice and vegetables in a fair pro- portion to the extent of land under cultivation. Owing to its antiquity, as Ei foreign settlement, Macao is a place of almost romantic interest. It was the resi- dence for five years of Louis Camoens, the famous author of "The Lusiad," during his banishment from Portugal. The poem, descriptive of Vasco di Gama's voyage of dis- covery round the Cape, is the great epic of the Portu- guese. The cave of Camoens, where the poet is supposed to have written his great work, is still pointed out, and is a place of universal resort. It is pleasantly situated , "in sweet retired solitude," with picturesque surroun- dings of granite rocks and oriental shrubbery, on the summit of a gently sloping hill, which overlooks the in- side harbour. The story of the poet's varied life is in..

Wresting. He was banished from Portugal about 1553, for aspiring to the hand of a lady of high rank, Catarina de Atavde. Proceeding to Goa, where he found the Governor already prejudiced, Camoens speedily became involved in trouble for writing satirical verses, and the publication of his "Absurdities of India" caused his banishment to the Moluccas. Macao afterwards became

his favourite residence, where his accomplishments and kindly disposition won to him many warm-hearted friends. Unfortunately, the poet was induced to return to Portugal, where he died in a public hospital in 1579; the last few years of life being spent in great misery. Within the present century, still remernbered by a few of the very old residents of Macao, Chinnery ,the artist had a home there, and many of the most valuable ,of his pictures were painted in Macao. The 'Centurion, under command of Commodore Anson, on her memorable voyage round the world, visited Macao in 1742. The first steamship to visit China arrived at Macao in 1830. Dr. Bridgman, the pioneer American missionary to China, notes the circumstance in his journal, May Ist :—"Arrived at Macao on the 19th (April), in the steamer Forbes, the first ship of the kind that has ever visited these shores. She's a wonder to the Chinese; they call her Fe Shune, the fire ship." The venerable author of "Morning of life in China," Mr. Gideon Nye, one of the old Canton merchants, informed the writer that the Forbes was most likely sent on from Italia with English official despatches. Hong Kong was not then used as an anchorage, and was not acquired until ten years later. On a Chinese drawing, repre- senting the English fleet attacking Canton in 1841, we find a curious description of a paddle-wheel steamer : " She's more than three hundred cubitsjong, And thirty-odd in height and breadth; Iron is used to bend her stiff and stout, And she's painted black all round about. Like a weaver's shuttle is her shape; On both sides carriage wheels are fixed, And, using fossil coal to make a fire, They whirl around as the racehorse ffies. Of white cloth all the sails are made, In winds both fair and foul she goes; On her bow is the god of the waves; At stem and stern is a revolving gun; , Her form is truly terrific to men. The god of the North displaying his sanctity, The sunken rocks there shoaled the steamer; All who saw it witnessed to the justice of Heaven. None of the plans of the foreigners took effect, Which greatly delighted the hearts of men." It is claimed for the Portuguese by Abbe Hue that Macao was ceded to them, several centuries ago, for capturing a notorious pirate who had long defied the Government of China. But the Chinese have always denied the claim, and still appoint an official from Canton to maintain jurisdiction over the Chinese population of Macao. The port of Amoy, in the southern province of Fuhkien, was opened to foreign trade in 1841, and is a place of great commercial importance; the city is large and • populous, and its merchants are remarkable for wealth and enterprise. The city stands on the south-west side of Hai-mun island, near the mouth of the Lung river; it is built but very little above the level of the sea, and its walls extend to the water side. The harbour is a fine one, formed between the indented shore of kulangsu island and a large estuary running some distanee into I the island of Hai-mun. Many ships visit the port; and large native junks can Sail close up to the houses, which cluster along the beach and overhang the water. The contiguous surroundings of Amoy are bleak and sterile- looking in the extreme; massy, precipitqus bulwarks of everlasting hills. "These hills contain some ancient tombs and sepulchres of great solidity, part of them being excavated out of rock ornamented with inscrip- tions and epitaphs; a mode of interment by no means common in China, nor even here used at present." The great granite rocks are conspicuous objects ; but we fail to see a sign of vegertation. On the south side of Amoy, some two or three miles before the harbour is reached, a large stone fort extends along a narrow strip of sandy beach, commanding the approach to the anchorage. _ The history of Amoy, in its relation to foreign trade, is interesting. The Portuguese visited, Amoy in the sixteenth century, and they carried on a large trade there until the Chinese expelled them. The expulsion of the Portuguese from Amoy is a prominent incident in the history of commerce with China. The authorities killed 450 Portuguese settlers, and burnt 13 of their ships which were in harbour. It is right to observe, in this case as in other instances, that the severe action against the Portuguese *as brought about by their arrogsnt demeanour towards the Chinese. Subsequently, the English established commercial relations with Amoy, and continued to send vessels there until 1730, when the Chinese Government declared Canton to be the only trading port open to foreigners in China. For some reason an exception was made in favonr of the Spaniards, yet they Availed themselves but little of the privilege. So—excepting unlawful traders under every national banner, or likely enough waving the black flag—Amoy remained a 'closed port until 1841, when the English military and naval forces, under the joint command of General Gough and Admiral Parker, captured the city and destroyed the fortifications. Amoy was declared an open port by the famous treaty of Nankin, signed on board the Cornwallis, August 29th, 1842. Very few foreigners reside on Hai-mun ; the native city, and the usual gathering of the villages outside the walls of Chinese cities, occupy that part of the island universally known as Amoy. Several fine temples are to, be found in the city"; and the most prominent buildings ootside, quite close to the harbour, are the Custom House, Missionary Hospital for Chinese, and other similar I structures. As a rule the people are well disposed towards foreigners, although we have heard dark stories of sailors being cruelly beaten in the narrow alleys outside the city. Our own experience of the natives of Amoy is _a favourable one. The men are mostly fine, well-built fellows, said to make excellent soldiers with a certain independent dash about them very unlike the general bearing of Chinese. Their independence is illustrated in the following incident, but many may be cited of their tenacity to old customs. When the Chinese of the Ming dynasty, about 1644, succumbed to the warlike incursions of the • Manchu Tartars (originally from the Amcor country), the people of Fuhkien were the last to submit to the rule of the invaders. The Tartar Emperor issued an edict ordering the Chinese to shave the head and adopt the queue, after the manner of the Manchus, as a mark of submission and allegiance. But it has been supposed the real meaning of the edict was to prevent the Chinese estimating the somewhat limited numbers of the conquering Tartars. Previous to the Tartar dynasty the Chinese wore long flowing hair,, a custom revived during. the late Tai-ping rebellion—hence the name given to the insurgent, Chongmeta, "long-haired men." To hide the sign of degradation imposed by the Tartars, the Amoy men wound turbans round their head, and to this day they adhere faithfully to the custom of wearing a turban,. a covering never seen in any other part of China. Perhaps Amoy deserves a word or two as a curiosity mart, where travellers may obtain many interesting additions to their collections, Shells cut and polished to resemble cat's eyes, dried beetles of variegated colours, polished stones for ornaments, cleverly-carved nutshells, and gnarled roots, out of which they make curious vases and grotesque images. The vendors of these articles are very numerous, and crowd round every ingoing ship long before the anchor is dropped. Amoy is also famous for artificial flowers, most beautiful imitations of the lily, rose, tulip, and convolvulus, made of the pith ob- tained from a plant allied to the Artocarpus, or bread- fruit. This delicate vegetable substance retains the most brillitnt colours in a marvellous degree, and we have known instances of these duplicates of Nature being ac- cepted as the real production. Those occupied in the manufacture of them , are men, women, and children of the poorest class, and splendid bunches of flowers may be purchased for a trifling sum. Kulang-su is a small island on which is built the foreign settlement. It is opposite the city of Amoy, from which it is separated by a deep water channel less than a third of a mile wide; the island is less than three mites in cir- cumference, and great granite rocks are scattered more or less over its whole uneven surface. After the first Anglo-Chinese war the island was garrisoned for a time by British troops, but no trace of their occupancy was allowed to remain. When the English soldiery. vacated the island the Chinese destroyed every sign that would be likely to remind them of the unwelcome visitors of 1841. Very few Chinese now live on the island beyond those employed by the foreigners. It has been almost entirely turned over to the small community of foreign residents, who have made good roads, built grand houses, arranged fine gardens in the shade of huge rocks; and we know of few more attractive places open to foreigners on the coast of China. We have already mentioned the stoppage of trade at Amoy in 1730. Before that time the vessels of the East India Company were constantly going to asSd fro; and in 1723 a somewhat celebrated personage, the writer of "A New Account of the East Indie," Captain Alexander Hamilton, loaded his ship at Amoy. On one of the least frequented corners of Kulang-su island, very near the water side, we still find memorials of some of those old ocean wanderers, who were laid to rest in that wild burial ground nearly two hundred years ago. Many of the gravestone inscriptions are almost obliterated, but we succeeded in tracing out four of the epitaphs which are not devoid"bf interest, and may be helpful sometime to the genealogist : (1.) div.p: ' MANCHESTER 'SHIP' CANAL BILL. MONDAY. . IMPORTANT INTIMATION. Mr. Marshall Stevens, of Liverpool, whose ex ,mination was begun late on Friday at, ernoon, complained of the de- lays which occur at Liverpool in the forwarding of goods to Manchester and inland towns. The traffic had increased enormously at Garston, where the dues were much below those charged at Liverpool, and there was now insufficient accommodation to meet the demand. It frequently hap- pened that a vessel had to wait two or three weeks for a berth. Continuing, Mr. Stevens said the saving at Garston on each ton of cotton as compared with Liverpool was 3s Id per ton, and there was also a large saving on coal. It was cheaper, in fact, for a ship to sail past Liverpool to Garaton, there to deposit her cargo, and then to forward it back to the Liverpool market. In his view the Ship Canal was the proper remedy for this state of things. It would be practically one continuona , dock from Manchester to Eastham, and goods could be transhipped at any point on the line of route. ,The canal would break down the existing monopoly in the carrying trade, and lead to the erection of works on the !oinks of the canal. After the adjournment for luncheon, the committee having in the meantime con- sulted together. The Chairman said : We are informed the House of Lords this year decided to hear the engineering evidence first upon the ground that that appeared to them the reason why the bill was lost last year in the House of Com- mons. Well, we are of opinion we had better hear the en- gineering evidence at once, and, unless you can show very good reason to the contrary, we will ask you to bring your engineering witnesses to-morrow morning. We also wish to say one word with regard to the commercial evidence. I am informed by the promoters that •there are 133 gentlemen they would like to call, and 14 of these have already bees heard. I may say that the time of the committee is at your service on the conditions under which House of Comtnons committees generally sit and we must not be supposed in anything we say to wish to shorten the proceedings on our account. I may say for myself I have no objection to give any.amount of labour out of which a result may be ex- pected to come, but Ido very much object to giving that labour perfectly usdessly ; moreover, lam informed that counsel on both sides wish this long fight to come to an end, and that there would ba general regret if the session ended before tke committee concluded. Whether that regret I would be felt as much by the gentlemen on my left (the op- , ponents) as by those on my right, I cannot tell, but judg- ing , from what I have heard they are both anxious the matter should come to an end. The committee of the House of Lords this year sat 30 daye. which is equal to 38 days in the Commons. If we are to sit the same number of days we shall be here till the 6th of August. It is for the promo- ' tete to consider whether the House of Commons will sit till I that time. I think the chances are that it will not. That is supposing there is nothing concerning the bill but the proceedings relating to the preamble. I need not tell the learned counsel we have not even consulted with one another as to the final result. Of course, yea must suppose the possibility that the preamble may be declared to be proved. In that case there would be ad- I ditional days taken up in arrangirg the clauses, and I am only within the mark when I state that if the promoters proceed at the rate they did before the Lords, and as they appear to be going on at now, the chances of the bilMeing passed thia,session are about nil. I have only one farther suggestion to make. We have had in Committee two Cr three very 'competent witnesses, sucn as Mr. Marshall Stevens and Mr. Adamson, and one or two otherc. From ' these the Oammitt-m can really 'find out what they have to say, and we think they ought to serve the ptrpose of the prometers as much as a number of witnesses, and evert more so. That is for the promoters to coniider. My own feeling is this—We have asked several questions ourselves and we have felt that when we get a mat whoespresents a teadingrpart of the case we bad better not let •lelm go until we had thoroughly understeod in our minds what he hat got to-cay. Thu Chairman, in conclusion, repeated that the l'Committee would take the engineering -evidence to- morrow, and raid that in the meantime the promoters would have an opportunity of considering what course they ought to pursue. Mr. Pember (leading counsel for the promoters) : I will undertake that Mr. Leader Williams, the engineer to :1 the caromottes, shall be put into the 'box tc-morrow menn- ing. I Mr. Stevons was further examined regarding the several ltiads of traffic which were likely to pass over the I canal, after which he was cross-examined by Mr. Potter. L

div.head: TUESDAY.
div.p: TUESDAY.

- - - Mr. Mcrshall Stevens was farther .cross-examined on nesday morning. Answering Mr_ Ledgard, Q C., he esti- mated tke revenue from the meal at ,double the figures given by Mr. Pember, and said he believed the traffic vould amount to 9,000.000 tons per ennum. Further questions being aeked on this point, Mr. Stevens stated that witnesses could be called whe would empress 'their belief that the traffic en the Shio Canal would exceed that of. Liverpool, which was 15,000.000 tons annually. At the close of Mr. Steven's examinetion, the promoters alect evidence on the engineering part of the case. Mr. Leader Williams being the first witness, he described the engineering features of the scheme. Speaking drat of thapertion between Basthant and itutmorn, he informed the Chairman, in answer to a quesbien,that he knew of no other instance of a canal skirting a tidal estuary. Wherever the canal passed through portions of the estuary there were •einbankments, and in these embankments there were open- ings for the tide to pass into the canal. As the tide ehbed the surclus water in the canal would fowelowly away. In rela- tion to the obstruction caused by the bar at the mouth of the estuary, the Chairman asked whether the idea had ever been mooted of making a canal through the bar itself. The wit- ness replied that various suggestions had been made for the Improvement of the bar, but the Dock Board, who were a trust pure and simple, had never -spent a penny upon it, whilst on the Tyne, Tees, and Clyde the bar had been done away with and the river improved. The Chairman asked Iwhether the sinking of a vessel would block the proposed canal, as was the case in the Suez Canal. The witness re. plied that even it a vessel sank in the middle there would be 1:-ttle difficulty in making room for other vessels, to pass by, }and by means of locks and sluices, which did not exist on the Suez Canal, the water could be lowered in order to raise a vessel.

div.head: WEDNESDAY.
div.p: WEDNESDAY.

Mr. Leader Williams, engineer to the promotera, continued kis explanation of the plans for the proposed canal. Ile trot put in evidence a table showing the number of hours in the year during which vessels of various draughts of water !could leave or enter the canal at Eastham. It appeared that with a 20ft. channel at the entrance, as proposed by the promotere, vessels of 10ft. draught could enter or leave at any hour, and vessels of nr I. draught could pass, with two -feet of water under the keel, for .41:7f0 hours in the year (the I total number of hours in one year being 8,760). At the Liverpool docks vessels of 1012. draught could enter or leave 1 for only 1,410 hours in the year, and 221 t. vessels for only 1,380 hours.—Asked by the Chairman what arrangements had been made in the event of new roads being required over the canal, Mr. Pernber replied that a new swing bridge pre-supposed a new road, and a new road could not be made without an Act of Parliament. The witeess, continuing, .stated that the probable speed of steamers using the canal would be five miles an hoar, and the distance from East- • ham to Manchester, allowing for lookage, would be accom- plished in nine hours. The witsess next explained the pro- ,pesed works in the estuary of the Mersey from Runcorn to ,Eastham.—Just before the rising of the Committee the Chairman asked the counsel for the opponents whether they would be willing to give their ceenter-case upon the en- gineering and estuary case immediately after that part of the case for the promoters had concluded.—Mr. Pope said the opponents suffered so much from the adoption of that course in the other House they had resolved if they could help it not to agree to a similar course in the Commons.— Mr. Bidder suggested that tst the close of the promoters' case the Committee might call upon the petitioners to pro- ceed immediately with their engineerieg evidence, and that would partly meet the object they had in view.

TH E CONSERVATIVE LEADERS. LORD SALISBURY. Lord ;Salisbury, the new Conservative Premier, was born at Hatfield, the family residence, in 1830, and is now consequently fifty-five years of age. In the early part of his career there seemed little pros- I pect of his succeeding to the title he now bears, but lon the death of his eldest brother, in 1865, he be- came heir to the maroisate, to which he succeeded in 4868. His Parliamentary career commenced in 1853, when he was but twenty-two years of age, by his being elected to represent Stamford.. He soon won a reputation as a keen debater, his style of oratory winning for him a reputation as a master of ",gibes and flouts and sneers." He was also a con- tributor to various periodicals, and especially the Raturday lievioto. In July, 1866, he was appointed :Secretary of State for India, in Lord Derby's Govern- ment, but resigned in the following year on.account of his strong opposition to the Reform Bill. When the Conservatives were returned to power in 1874, Lord Salisbury twain became head of the India Department; and °on differences arising between Russia and Turkey he was despatched to Constanti- nople as special Ambassador, but on the Conference breaking up he returned to England without having settled the differences. In 1878 Lord Derby resigned his post of Foreign Secretary in the Beaconsfield Cabinet owing to its warlike policy, and Lord Salis- bury was installedin the vacant office. As Foreign Secretary he accompanied Lord Beaconsfield to the Berlin Congress, and on his return, along with his chief, he was invested with the Order of the Garter by the Queen. After the death of Lord Beaconsfield, in 1881, Lord Salisbury was elected the leader of Ithe party in the House of Lords. In 1857 he married Georgina Caroline, daughter of Sir Edward Hall Anderson, Baron of the Exchequer, by whom he has ' had eight children. SIR STAFFORD NORTIICOTE. After having occcupied a seat in the House of Commons for about thirty years, and having been the leader of his party in that Chamber since Lord Beaconsfield was raised to the peerage, Sir Stafford INorthcote has now, either voluntarily or involun- tarily, followed the example of his late chief, and' will in future be known by the unfamiliar name of Lord Iddesleigh. Sir Stafford was born on October 270.818, and is the eldest son of the late Henry Stafford Northeote, Esq. He was educated at Eton 1 and Oxford, and graduated first class in classics and third class in mathematics. While Mr. Glad- stone was President of the Board of Trade in 1843-5, Sir Stafford acted as his private secretary. He was returned to Parliament for Dudley .in March, 1855, and subsequently sat for Stamford from July, 1858, till May, 1866, when he was elected for North , Devon, for which constituency he has been returned at every succeeding general election. In 1866 he was appointed President of the Board of Trade in Lord Derby's administration, and from March, 1867, till Decembero.B7B, he was Secretary for India. In. 1874 he was nominated Chancellor of the Exche- quer, which office he held during the whole course of the Beaconsfield Government. Sir Stafford has tried his hand at authorship, his first publication' being " The ease of Sir. Eardley Wilmot, considered in a letter to a friend," which is a vindication of the action of his old chief, Mr. Gladstone, in recalling Sir Eardley Wilmot from Van Dieman's Land. His other works were "A Statement of Facts connected with the election of the Right Hon. W. E. Gladstone as Member for the University of Oxford in 1874, and on his re-election in 1852 and 1853," and certain treatises on financial subjects. In 1843, Sir Stafford married Cecilia, daughter of Thomas Farrer, Esq., of Lincoln's Inn. SIR• M. HICKS-BEACH. The new leader of the Tory party in the House of Commons, is eldest son of the late Sir Michael Hicks Hicks-Beach, of Williamstrip Park, Gloucestershire. He was born in London in 1837. In 1864 he was elected to Parliament for East Gloucestershire, a constituency he still represents, and in 1868 he was Parliamentary secretary to the Poor Law Board, and for a few weeks Under Secretary for the Home Department. In 1874 he was appointed Chief Sec- retary for Ireland, but on the resignation of Lord Carnarvon in 1878, he was transferred •to the Colonial Office. Although Sir Michael is said to be popular and influential in the part of the country ; with which he is more immediately connected, in Ithe north he is probably one of the least known leaders of the Tory party. Of late, he has been rather more to the fore, owing to his being selected to submit some of the• most important resolutions which his party have formulated in Parliament, and more particularly that over which Mr. Glad- stone's Government came to grief. Although by no means a great orator, his friends claim for him considerable capacity for debate, and more than ordinary administrative ability. Sir Michael is a magistrate and deputy-lieutenant of Gloucester- shire, and was formerly a captain of the militia. LORD RANDOLPH CHURCHILL. Lord Randolph Churchill, who is looked upon by a large section of Conservatives as the "rising hope " of their party, is, when compared with the general run of leading politicians, a very young man, having been born in 1849, and consequently is only 36 years of age. Ile is the son of the late Duke of Marlborough, and was first introduced to Parliament through the family borough of Wood- stock, in 1874, and has to the present time con- tinued to represent that constituency, which is one of those that will disappear when the new Redistri- bution Bill comes into operation. The early part of his Parliamentary life was comparatively quiet and uneventful, but since the election of 1880, and more particularly since the death of Lord Beaconsfield, he has been acquiring an increasingly potent voice in the management of his party. At the present time he is undoubtedly the most popular man on the ensere leadervx aten vpoelf side of opbfya the House, r yi aplaees appointment the value which the on his Cbe°nhis to services r by ie ce s h se cr ae q_ -tary of State for India, one of the most responsible of positions. He is one of the most effective speakers, and probably the readiest debater on the Conservative side, while outside, not even his titular leader, Lord Salisbury, can draw larger audiences. Lord Randolph is married to the daughter of Mr.. L. Jerome, a New York millionaire. SIR RICHARD CROSS. The new Home Secretary, Sir Richard Cross, the member for South-west Lancashire, was born at Red sear, near Preston, in 1823, being the third son of the late William Cross, Esq. In 1849 he was realled to the bar at the Inner Temple, and for I several years he went to the northern circuit. In 11852 he married Georgina, daughter of the late Thomas Lyon, Esq, of Appleton Hall, near War- rington. He was first elected member of Parlia- ment for Preston in 1857, and represented that borough till 1862. In 1868 he contested South-west Lancashire against Mr. Gladstone, and was &turned head of the poll. In 1874 he was appointed Home Secretary, which Zee he held till 1880, when he
SIR MICHAEL HICKS BEACH.
