A TORY ON THE TORY POLICY. Mr. James Lowther, addressing a meeting of his con- stituents at Market Rosen on Tuesday evening, said he frankly confessed be was unable to answer definitely the question as to what Government was in office at the present time. He sincerely trusted that what he bad not hesitated previously to describe as a national calamity, namely, the acquisition to power nominally of any new Ministry which did not possess real power, backed by the majority of the House of Commons, might even yet be averted. In his judgment it was contrary to the fundamental principles of the English Constitution that any Ministry should hold office unless it could either command the majority of the existing House of Commons or be in a position to tender constitutional advice to the Sovereign to enable an appeal to be made to the country. No Government formed by the Conservative party could do either of these things. Conse- quently he clung to the hope that they would be spared what he should consider the national calamity of a Conser- vative Government unbrcked by a Conservative majority in the House of Commons. SIR CHARLES DILKE ON THE SITUATION. Sir Charles Ddke was the principal speaker on Mouday night at a meeting held in Chelsea to consider the revision of the rules and constitution of the Chelsea Liberal AS9oCia- lion to meet the altered circumstances brought about by the Redistribution Bill.—Sir Charles said he could not treat Sir M. Hicks-Beach's speech except as one in favour of taxing tea, and he could not for one moment admit that a duty of 50 per cent. on tea could be said to be moderate. (Cheers.) Of course, Sir M. Hicks-Beach had since been disavowed, and had, indeed, disavowed himself, and, of course, also, the Conservative party would, if they took office, adopt the heroic course of borrowing all the money needed in order that the Liberals might have to pay it off next year. One of the reasons why the very able and blameless leader of the Conservative party In the House of Commons had been driven from his place by intrigue, and by which Sir M. Hicks-Beach had profited, was because he was trained at the feet of Mr. Gladstone, and was in favour of sound prin. ciples of finance. (Hear, bear.) In the Conservative news- papers last Thursday there was a paragraph announcing that Lord R. Churchill made no stipulations or condi- tions, on agreeing to accept office, and that the reports published to that effect were without founda- tion. What ! No stipulation, for example, an to Ireland with his well-known opinions on that subject. Was the noble lord so soon as he got his way about per. eons content to leave that serious question to chance and to accept without conditions the rule of Lord Cernarvon, an amiable but rather narrow nobleman? eine° the founda- tion of the new Government a little inquiry had been made upon this subject ef Ireland. A paragraph had appeared in the press headed "Coercion Bill,' and announcing that a lithograph circular, addressed from the Conservative Cen- tral Offices, St. Stephen's Chambers, Westminster, had been received by a prominent Conservative in the city of Chester. signed "Richard W. Middleton "—a gentleman who suc- ceeded Mr. Bartley as party manager—asking for informa- tion respecting the approximate number of Irish voters in Chester, and also for an opinion whether the Conservative and Radical parties were so evenly divided that the Irish vote would give a majority to one side or to the other. Who gave orders for that circular? What did it mean? (Hear. hear.) Was it that the policy which was to guide the Con- servative party in this matter was to be calculated by coun- ting voters' heads ? The circular was sent out from Lan- I don on Tuesday last, the day that Sir S. Northcote had been driven from the leadership of the Conservative party ia the House of Commons, and the day on which Lord R. Churchill accepted office without conditions. He thought .he might leave them to draw their own conclusions. (Hear. hear.) It was now rumoured that the Conservatives would not take office unless they received from the Liberals most formal and precise aseurances of support. Many membere of the Liberal party argued that they deserved no considera- tion; but the interests of the country must stand first. For himself he would be prepared to give all reasonable assurances for stronger assurances than ever before were asked for or given but they were not prepared to go fur- ther than they had done. (Cheers.) It was the in- tention of Mr. Chamberlain and himself to give up the earliest holiday which they could make to inquiry in Ire- land of those who knew Ireland best. The provincial Tory newspapers declared that they intended to try and compel the concession of their terms by banging up the Seats Bill and by threatening to upset it by dissolving before it bad been passed. This was a game of brag. They did not and could not intend to annihilate the very bill the obtaining of which constituted what they called their triumph; and the Liberal pary need not be concerned at the menace of an Impossible dissolution. To dissolve on the present register, with the old franchise and the old distribution of seats (as Lord Salisbury threatened), after all that had passed, would amount to an outrage on the Constitution. (Cheers.) Once upon a time, Liberate were told that to have a new fran- chise without redistribution would be the destruction of the Tory party, yet that was what they would be face to face with on January Ist if they dissolved and threw out the Redistribution Bill. It was an idle and an empty threat. Liberals did not expect consistency from Conservatives, but knew they dare not carry ont their threat. The loss of the Seats Bill would be extremely inconvenient to the country, but happily the Franchise Act was safe. The postpene- ! ment of the Redistribution Bill action wash ardly calculated Ito encourage the Liberals incautiously to give unprecedented assurances or to venture on a formal compact with the other side. (Loud cheers.) THE CHANGE OF GOVERNMENT. Lord Randolph Churchill was the first of the new Minis- try to assume the duties of his post, reaching the Indian Office at balf-past eleven on Thursday morning The next Minister in Downing-street was Sir Michael Hicks-Beach, who entered the Treasury at a quarter to twelve. Colonel Stanley, a little later, visited the Colonial Office, and Lord George Hamilton took over his duties at the Admiralty at noon. Sir Henry Holland arrived at the Treasury shortly after that hour, and assumed the duties of Financial Secre- tary. Lord Arthur Hill, on Thursday, accepted the Con- trollership of the Household. This will cause a vacancy for County Down. It is understood that Mr. Bariacton, of the Foreign Office, will act as one of Lord Salisbury's private secretaries. Lord Cranbourne, the Premier's eldest son, will act in a like capacity. Sir iiardinge Gifford was on Thursday sworn in the Court of Appeal as the new Lord , Chancellor with the due and usual formalities. Mr. Gladstone has left Downing-street and nice° up his residence at the house of Mr. Bertram Currie, Rich mond- terrace, for the remainder of the session. Sir Stafford Northcote, on Thursday, took over No. 10. Downing-street, the official residence of the First turd of the Treasury, and Sir Michael Hicks-Beach, who is Chancellor of the Ex- chequer, occupies one of the two houses in which Mr. Gladstone resided. Lord George Ilemilton assumed office as First Lord of the Admiralty on Thursday after- noon. A meeting of the Conservative members of both Hovel I was held at the Carlton Club at half-past two en Thursday afternoon, to bear a statement from the Prime Minister of the reason which had induced him to take office. The attend- ance of both peers and commoners was unusually large. Long before two o'clock members had begun to assemble, and among the earlier arrivals were Mr. James Lowther and Lord Cranbrook. Lord Salisbury arrived at 25 minutes after two, and was followed by Sir Steff ird Northcete. The last arrivals did not reach tne Club until a quarter to three. when the meeting commenced. Lard Saiiebury explained why he had taken office, and received what was practically a unanimous vote of confidence. Sir S. Northcote had a speciary cordial reception from the meeting. A Paris correspondent says f—An exch mge of views is taking place between the Cabinets of Paris and St. Peters- burg relative to the foreign policy of the Salisbury Ad- ministration. lam able to say on the best authority that at the same time M. Waddington has been instructed to sound Lord Salisbury as to what his views and intentieno are regarding Egypt. The Queen has been pleased to confer a peerage on Mr. Rowland Winn, M.P., under the :style of Baron St. Oswald. of Hostel), in the county of York. Mr. Wine's seat was vacated on Thursday afternoon by his acceptance of the Chiltern. Hundreds.

On Thursday morning a fire occurred at the works of Messrs. Newsome, West, and Co., DeweburS, and damage was done to the amount of £20,000. The hien Artisans' Exhibition was opened in Dublin on Wednesday. It embraces exhibits in almost every branch of the Irish industry and manufacture. A report that the Duke of Marlborough intended to pre- vent if possible the return of Lord It. Churchill (his I brother) for Woodstock is contradicted by the Duke him- self. , the Conservatives will attempt anything heroic in the way of legislation S; they will not even trouble themselves to renew the Crimes Act, although coercion has always been a cardinal article of their creed. They will prefer, after beginning by abusing the Liberals for going on the wrong track with regard to Ireland, to end by going on the same track—that is as far as it is in their power to follow it. They will not do much work of any kind; the work of the present Parliament is done, and it stands to the credit of the retiring PRIME MINISTER, who has carried the greatest measure of reform that this country has known. The Tories are coming in to look at the furniture, and "dust down" prior to its being decided who has to hold the lease on the new and enlarged house. They will be sufficiently occupied in doing what the Liberals permit them, and in eating their own words. There is a rumour that Russia will demand explanations of Lord SALISBURY and Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL, and, if this be true, it may lead to something awkward. Not.that either politician will not be prepared to explain away his wild words —Lord SALISBURY has already attempted the operation—but it is just possible that it may lead to a re-opening of the breach which Mr. GLADSTONE has so skilfully closed. It is as well to have our eyes open to the fact that it is in their foreign policy that the Tory Ministry are most likely to go wrong. Meantime they must be judged on their merits and dealt with fairly. As is customary with another illustri- ous personage, we must give Lord SALISBURY his due.

THE Address of Mr. GOSCHEN, M.P., on he condition of trade, delivered on Tuesday before the members of the Manchester Chamber of Commerce, has enhanced his reputation for grappling with financial pro- blems and for the thoroughness with which he cirries out anything he takes in hand. It was not his intention, as some might have anticipated, to deal with the question of Fair Trade; Mr. GOSCHEN is.not one of those to employ his energies, on such an occasion, in flogging a dead horse. He had nothing startlingly new to say; but he was in a posi- tion to disperse some hazy misconceptions, and to make clear some things that have been too much kept in the dark. There is and has been depression in trade—that is patent to everybody; but, when that is admitted, it remains to be said that things are not so bad as they are generally pictured. Particular industries have suffered, such as iron, cotton, and mining; there has been a diminution of profit; but no diminution in the volume of trade. With regard to the cotton trade, pf which we hear so inueh in Lancashire, Mr. GoscilgN was in a position to show that, bad as it is, capitalists are not afraid to risk their money in it. The total number of spindles, which was 4.4.,z00,000 in 1879, was nearly 47,000,000 in 1883 ; while the number of persons employed in the trade in those four years rose from 483,000 to 513,000. It is an economic law that capital ceases to flow into any given chan- nel when it is not profitably employed and when there is no hope of its becoming profitable. We must, therefore, conclude that cotton manufacturers are working upon past profits and, present hopes. The well may he getting low, but there is consolation in their case in knowing that it sometimes fills rapidly. There is one highly satisfactory feature in, connection with the present as compared with past bad times, and that is that the prices of food are low. Wages, on the other hand, have kept tolerably well up; indeed, it is not uncommon for capitalists to say that the only classes who are doing well are the working classes. By way of answer, however, to this observatian it is but fair to point to what Mr. ,GOSCHEN calls " the astounding statistics under the name of income tax returns." In fifteen years the gross returns of the income tax have risen from [470,000,000 to boo,ooo,ocio. A nation may not be making a maximum profit; but it cannot be said to be getting poorer, in face of such an increase, in a short period, in the returns for tax-paying purposes. Mr. GOSCHEN proceeds to show that a large sum has been swallowed up in augmented rents, railway profits, &c, leaving little, compara- tively, for trade pure and simple. But he made a suggestive 'exception as to the retail trade, observing that "it had undoubtedly been greatly flourishing, and was flourish- ing now." Dealing with the lessons to toe learned from the past, he instanced the case of Bradford, which had once been un- sound on the question of Free Trade. Its manufacturers wanted " Protecting " when they found that they were losing their hold upon continental markets. For a time they were in despair; but they finally set them- selves to face the difficulty, and had at last overcome it. They had improved their methods and machinery; and brought more skill and intelligence to their work. The result was that they could now more than hold their own, and Bradford was flourish- ing. In .the course of his most valuable addrns, Mr. GOSCHEN referred to the tests of the prosperity of a country, and we conclude With an in'eresting extract on this important Point. He said : What other tests were there? There was one which it was impossible to pass by, and that was the ques- tion of the consuming powers of the country. With regard to these, the statistics were decidedly satis- factory. The people had drunk more tea than in any previous year, they had consumed more sugar, travelled more miles, consumed more wool and cot- ton in their manufactims, employed as many ser- vants, taken out as many licenses to shoot, and had as many carriages. In none of those great depart- ments Of elpenditure, whether touching the work- ing classes or the well-to-do, was there any sign of falling-off in consumption or use excepting one, and that was in the consumption of spirits. (Hear, hear, and a laugh.) There the decline was notable. We drank now only ten glasses of spirits for every thirteen that we drank in the greatest drink- ing year, which was the year 1875, and we had cut off one glass out of every ten even during the last four or five years. In tobacco there was a very slight decrease. We had cut off one pipe or cigar out of every 35, and that was sup- posed to he due partly to the higher duty. Almost in every direction, except where other explanations were given, such as the greater temperance of the people and the exertions made in that cause, there was a positive increase in the consuming powers of the country. We have only to add that the country of which all this can be said is not yet going to the dogs.

SIR CHARLES DrLKE, speaking at a large meeting .of Liberals in Chelsea, on Monday, did justice to an opponent in exposing the unprincipled character of the intrigue by which Sir STAFFORD NORTHCOTE has been driven from the leadership of the House of Commons He called it, he said, an intrigue, because it was not a fair fight followed by a fair victory it was underhand, and had to do with persons rather than principles. It was part of the outcome of what one Conservative paper referred to as the "gratuitous and mischievous mutiny " of Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL. The lordling has dictated, and now that " the blameless leader " has been

elbowed cut of the way the Tories will per- haps begin to ask themselves what better they are for the change. It will be some little con- solation to Sir STAFFORD NORTHCOTE to re- member the ringing cheers with which he was received on the Liberal side of the House when he took his place the night after what was regarded as his deposition. As a rule, when a politician is applauded by his oppo- nents he has said or done something suspi- cious, if not discreditable; but no one can suggest this of Sir STAFFORD NORTHCOTE. It was the ill-usage of his " friends" that pro- voked a counter demonstration from his oppo- nents. It was felt that, whatever might be urged Rs to his failing as a leader, it could still be said that— thus he bore without abuse The grand old name of gentleman— without abuse so far as he himself is con- cerned, though everybody knows he has been subjected to not a little abuse from the arch- intriguer who is now using Sir MICHAEL HICKS-BEACH as a stop-gap till the time comes when he can leap into his place. Sir STAFFORD NORTHCOTE goes, therefore, to the House of Lords ; if he had been twenty years younger he would have followed where his instincts would lead him—into the ranks of the Liberal party. Another interesting feature of the speech of Sir CHARLES DILKE was his reference to the announcement which has been made of his intended visit to Ireland, along with Mr CHAMBERLAIN, with the ob- ject of ascertaining how local self-government may be extended, not only in Ireland, but in Scotland and Wales. It is characteristic of him that he should speak of the oppor- tunity of such work as "a rest" from the cares of office, and " a holiday." It is noteworthy, too, that he does not hesitate to let it be known that "some of the ablest and fairest men who have ever held the office of Viceroy" by no means approve of what is generally termed " Castle " Government as the best for Ire- land. We are on the eve of great changes as the result of Democracy feeling its feet; and if Irishmen will be patient and persevere, and be true to those who have given them so much under the Administration of Mr. GLAD STONE, there is reason to hope that Home Rule of one kind or another will be granted them. The fact is Parliament has got too much to do; and, having more than it can properly manage, some work is " scamped " and other work is left hopelessly in atrear. We want more of Home Rule—or, in other words, sub-division of labour—in every part of the United Kingdom.

div.p: THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, JUNE 27, 1885.

WIDNES POLICE Comm—Yesterday a man named Jos. Brawley was brought tip at this court, before Mr. Brock, and fined 5s and costs for being drunk. He went to prison for seven days in default of payment. PROMOTION AT RllNCORN.—Sergeant McMichael, who for the past five . years bas been stationed in the Rancorn division, has been promoted to the position of sergeant in charge at Malpas, and commences his new duties on Monday next. Sergeant McMichael leaves many friends behind in Runcorn. PRIMITIVI METHODIST CHAPEL, Hawow.-0.1 Sunday last sermons were preached in the above pla6 of worship, afternoon and evening, by Mr. T. Rollinson, of SIIIIO3'S Cross.' Collections were made in aid of the trust fund, .and amounted to the sum of £3 10s. The sermons were bath instructive and interesting. Mr. Peter Clare presided at the organ.. Mg ALLEGED 'HEFT FROM A. COMMERCIAL TRAVELLER. —AI Widnes Petty Bessions'on Monday, Robert Neill and George Jackson, described as professional theives, were brought before Mr. Brock,on remand, charged with stealing a briar wood pipe and coo from a Liverpool commercial traveller named Boyd, on the 13th inst. A further remand was granted, the addresses given by the prisoners, which had been communicated with, having revealed the fact that the persons written to knew nothing ablut The two men. FLOWER SERVICE AT RUNCOEN.—On Sunday, a flower service Was held at Bethesda Congregational Chapel, Run- corn' when the Rev. J. D. •Thomas preaehed from the words "The flowers appear on the earth." The building bad been prettily decorated by young ladies aed gentlemen of the congregation, under the superintendence of Messrs. W. H. Chadwick and R. Wyllie. Flowers were carried to the homes of various sick persons in the town after tne ser- vice, and the remainder have been forwarded to the Widnes Accident Hospital and to the Liverpool lofirmary. FOUND DROWNED INTER CANAL.—On Wednesday morn- ing the body of a man named John Allen (24),a lorry driver in the employ of the M. S. di L. Railway, who had been living at Terracewoad. Widnes, was found in the canal near the Iron Bridge, by a man who was engaged discharging sand. At about ten o'clock on Friday night deceased left a public-house in Anne-street West, for the purpose of going home, and it is supposed that he fell into the canal and was drowned.—Mr. Husband, deputy coroner, and a jury, in. quired into the circumstances of the case yesterday, when a verdict of "Found drowned "was returned. THEFT FROM WIDNES METAL WORKS. At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, a disreputable-looking man named James Keating was charged with stealing 14Ibs weight of copper, value 101., from the Widnes Metal Works, On the previous day.—William. Harper, foreman at the works in question, deposed to seeing prisoner go out of the works by the large gateway, carrying something that was apparently heavy under his arm. He afterwards saw pri- soner bury something in some sand. Keating had no business on the premises.—Thomas Richard Warne, re- finer at the metal works, proved fading a quantity of metal at a place indicated by his foreman, which he idenUfi-cl as befog the property of his masters.—Prisoner, who made no reply be the charge, was committed to the sessions for trial.

RUNOORN BURIAL BOARD.--.A meeting of rateplvers Was held on Thursday night in Bethesda Schoolroom, Runcorn, for the purpose of electing three members of the Runcorn Burial Board, in place of Messrs. Peter Briscoe, Wislfam Whittaker, and William Mellor. Mr. W. Handley presided, and the public were represented by two ratepayers and the Vestry Clerk. The Chairman read a letter from Mr. Brie- coe,in which be stated that on account of ill-health he did not seek re-election. It was resolved that a letter be sent to Mr. Briscoe regretting that be could not any longer per- form the duties of the office' and thanking him very cor- dially for his past services. Messrs. W. Whittiker and W. Mellor were re-elected, and Mr. Elward Imison was ap- pointed in place of Mr. Briscoe. A vote of thanks to the chairman terminated the proceedings. " ONWARD " JUVENILE Tgams.—The weekly gathering of the members of thislemple was held on Tuesday evening, in the Matins Temperance Hall, SiMOVEI Cross. Three juveniles were initiated, and one sister of the adult lodge was initiated as honorary member. The superintendent (Bro. J. Thompson) distributed some book prizes, which had been,presented by Bro. T. Reay, to be given to thos chil- dren who had brought the largest number of children to the temple. The first prizes were won by Bro. R. Phillips. CT, and Sister Mrggie Hirrison, ?,. And the ether real- , pients were Sisters Emma Roberts and Miry Ann illl and Bro. R. Jenkins. Bro. R. Jenkins proposed, and Sister Maggie Harrison secOnded, a vote of thanks to Bro. Reay for hie kindnese, which was heartily accorded. Recitation. were afterwards given by Sisters E. Roberts and E. Loines. and a reading by Sister M. Harrison. - Puren Lama Burma, Is pe,r ih— S hV LAWLESS Bncrramts. 5, Market-place, Watrington.—Advt.

RUNCORN POLICE CouRT—AL this court, on Thursday. before Captain Hazlehurst, Jane Dean was charged with stealing several articles of clothing, the property of Chad,e Frederick Elkins, Suffolk-street, under circsmstances pre- viously narrated. The prisoner was also charged with ob- taining a pair of boots from Mrs. Stone, wife of Henry Stone, boot and shoe, maker, by means of false pretences. It appeared that on Saurday, the 13th inst., the prisoner was sent by Mrs. Edkins to pay Mr. Stone for a pair of boots obtained some days previously. She then stated that Mrs. E Nine had told her to take hack another pair, for which she would pay later on. Mrs. Stone' let the prisoner have tha beets, but it transpired that Mrs. Edkius know nothing wha ever of the transaction, and it was discovered that the prisoner had caused the boots to be pledged at the shop of Mr. 'raison, Church-street. —The prisoner was committed for trial on both charges. " AsiAuLT IN* A RAILWAY CARRIAGE.—Qa Monday, it Runcorn Petty Sessions, an Irish harvestman named Patrick , Carroll was brought up on a charge of interfering with the comfort of passengers in a carriage belonging to the Londou ' and North-Western Railway Co.—Enoch Sefton, living at Mill Brow, said he was a passenger on Saturday night by the train which left Lime street at five minutes past six. As soon as the train started the prisoner, who was in the same compattment, 'commenced to swear, and challenged anyone in the carriage to fight him. No one interfered with him. Shortly afterwards he began to talk to a companion in the Irish language, and as soon as the train got over Runcorn Bridge the prisoner struck him heavily in the eye with his fist. ils bad not been able to see since with that eye.—The prisoner said he had had some drink, and was sorry for what he had done.—He was also charged with assault, and the Bench fined him 109 and costs on each charge, or an alternative in each case of 14 days' imprison- ment.

THE BuTTERINE Qtmsnota.—At Widnes Pelts' Seed ens, on Wednesday, Mr. J. eollitt, grocer and provision dealer, Widnes and Runcorn, was summoned for selling, on the Bth inst., one pound of butter not of the nature, quality, and substance .lemanded. Oa that day P.C. 221, iii plain clothes, visited a shop kept by the defendant in Lugsdale- road, Widnes. From a boy in the shop he purchased a pound of butter for 101, and ticketed at 10d. He then said it would be sent for analysis. Underneath tbe figures 10,1 was the word " butteripe," but that was not pointed out to him before he made the purchase. The result of the analy- sis was that the sample .of butter contained 6i per cent or water and 75 per cent of fatdeived from flesh. In defence Mr. Pollitt said that his assistants had instructions only to sell the mixture as batterine, and to have it labelled an such. The manager had been temporarily called away, and the sale was made by the boy ; otherwise the case would not have arisen. The magistrates thought that the case would be met by ordering defendant to pay the costs, 245. They advised him to mark the word butterine on the tickets in larger letters. ' FRODSHM PARISH CHURCH TowEn.—A meeting of the parishioners in the parish of Frodsham was held in the Kingsley Chapel. at the Parish Church, on Thursday morn. log, " for the purpose of passing such resolutions for the restoration or repair of the church tower as thel parishioners in vestry assembled may deem fit." The Rev. H. B. Blogg, (vicar) presided, and there were also present—Rev. Charley (curate), Mr. A. Thomas (churchwarden), Meests. H. Lineker' T. Davies, F. Rigby, R. Holland, H. G. Lan. aker, R. Ashton, T. Lewis, J. Robinson, S. Davies, J. Cunnah, T. Riley, J. Ashton, R. Bate, and J. Pollard.— Mr. Thomas stated that the sum of £379 had been promised for the restoration or repair of the towar, but there were Several subscribers to the rebuilding fund he had been un- able to communicate with owing to their absence from home.—The Chairman said that the churhwardens and him- self wished to have the opinion of toe vestry as to what action should be taken in regard to the church lower. It was a great disadvantage not to have the church belle, and they must try and have them again as soon as p.assi his.— Mr. H. Linaker said he thought the churchwardens should have been prepared to submit a scheme to the vestry, as the vestry knew nothing as to the condition of the tower except from the reports of Mr. Thomas Davies and Mr. Crowther, which were essentially the same.—Mr. Tnomes remarked that the churchwardens suggested Mr. Crowther and Mr. Samuel Davies should be appointed architects.— Mr. F. Rigby said that he had observed from the minutes that Messrs. Bodley and Gardner had been rejected, and as the restoration of the church in every sense of the word had been eminently successful, he thought the restoration of the tower should also be carried out by then. He pro- posed that the resolution passed at the last meeting reject- ing Messrs. Bartley and Gardner be rescinded.—Mr. John Ashton, in seconding the resolution, said he qaite agreed wit's Mr. Rigby.—A discussion ensued, and on the motion being put to the meeting it was negatived by six votes to three, but several members of the vestry did not vote.—lt was resolved that Mr. Samuel Davies, of Frodsbant, he ap- pointed architect for the restoration of the church tower, with Mr. Crowther, of Manchester, as consulting architect. A committee was appointed to raise the necessary funds and to carry out the work of restoration. RE-OPENING : NEW CLASSES NOW FORMING.—SMART AND COMPANY'S ANNUAL VISIT TO WAREINGTON.—SMart and Company, experienced teachers of rapid writiNebook-keep- ing, ;and shorthand, beg to announce the re.opening of their academy on Friday next, July 3rd. Apply at once fer a prospectus, to be had at any time at the grocer's shop ,t the Co-operative Stores, Sankey-street. Pierpoint Private Ralph Ratbbone BAZAAR AT DITTON —On Thursday, at Ditton, a bazaar in connection with St. Michael's Church was opened by the Mayer of Liverpool (Alderman Ratcliffe). The bazaar had been got up for the purpose of providing the church with a new organ and heating apparatus. It was held in the school-room, which was fitted up with a number of stalls which were presided over as follows :—First, Mrs. Woell and several assistants; second, Mrs. A. E. Smith, Mrs R. Lewe, Miss Payne; third, Miss Stcrev aud the vicar's chil- dren ' • fourth, Sunday school teachers; fifth (dairy produce), Mrs. MOSS and Miss Longton ; sixth (flowers), Mrs. Glover, Miss A. Turton, and Miss Whitehurst ; seventh (live stock), the choristers; eighth (refreshments), under the superinten- dence of Mrs. Berg'. The Mayor of Liverpool was accom- panied by Mrs. R.tcliffe, and there were also present—The Rev. C. W. Woell, Mrs, Wool', Rev. J. Wright Williams, Mrs. Williams, Rev. A. P. H. Wilson, Rev. G. Bond and Miss Bond, Miss Haddock, Mr. and Mrs. J. White, Mr. and Mrs. Lucas, Major Cress, Mr. A. E. Smith, MW Hallows, Miss Lucas, Mr. and Mrs. Ferguson, Mrs. Leather. The Widnes Soap Works Brass Band was in attendance. The Rev. C. W. Wooll, in an opening address said that the object of the bazaar was to raise funds to obtain an organ and improved heating apparatus, two very necessary things for a place of worship. Tnat church had been there fifteen years, with a capital organ chamber' which had up to the present time been unoccupied. When he came to that parish of course he c .uld clearly see an organ was required, and he could else see that the attendance at the 'church was considerably marred in winter through the want of a heat- ing apparatus. He also referred to the peculiar circum- stances of the parish, in which there were 1,500 people, of whom 500 were Roman Catholics, from whom of course they I received no assistance. They had no wealthy class in Dit- ton, and all the tithes went outside the parish.—The Mayor of Liverpool then opened the bazaar with an appropriate speech. The bazaar was opened yesterday, and will be open to-day. ASSAULT BY A BUILDER AT RUNCORN.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday James Farrell, a builder, was cnarged with unlawfully assaulting Miss Leah Peacock, of 20, Lord- street, on the 17th inst.—Mr. Livesey, solicitor, of Derby, appeared for the complainant,'ancl Mr. Lake (Messrs. Day and Lake) far the defendanr.—The complainant said that on Wednesday evening she WAS standing opposite the house of Miss Leach, in Mersey-view. While there she saw the defendant's father come out with a dog and run some boys off. She used words of expostulation to Sir. Farrell, who replied that it would serve the boys right if they were bitten. Defendant then came out and used bad language, saying that if she did not move from the place he would move her with his foot. She ttild him he dare not do so, when be seized her by the shonlders, pushed her across the road, and knocked her down on the parapet. By Mr. Lake : She was not leaning with her friends against the fence which protected the road from a lower one. She did not use irritating language. She had never been complained of the people living in Mersey-view for being on the road.— Mr. Lake pointed out that the road where the alleged assault took place was a private one, and the tenants living there had suffered great annoyance through boys using the place as a kind of playground, and young men and women using it as a lovers' walk. On the evening in question Mr. Farrell. the owner of the properly, eraered a number of boys away. One of the boys ran for protection behind Miss Peacock, and she screened him. Mr. Farrell told her she had na right there, and ordered her to leave. Instead of quietly going away the complainant insulted Mr. Farrell, and told him she would not go for him or anyone like him. The defendant was very much irritated on hearing his father insulted, and told her plainly if she did not move he would move her. There was great provocation, and the defendant had to move her. He held that the complainant WAS a tremasser, and that no more violence than was justifialde under the cir- cumstances had been used.—Mr. Williain Farrell, builder, contractor, and property owner, gave evidence in support of this statement. The road belonged to him, and he had re- ceived numerous complaints from his tenants about the an- noyance to which they were subjected by people standing In front of the houses —By the Cnairman : Miss Leach had a right to be on the road because she was a tenant, but he could not say whether any of her friends had any ri;ltt to be there.—The Bench considered the case preyed. It ,was clear that the complainant did not know that the road was a private one, and even if she had she had a right to speak toher friend who lived there. The defeadaut would be fined 103 and 18s costs.

MYSTERiOUS DEATH AT WIDNES.—John Edwardson (26), a plumber and painter, who lived at 44, Midwood-street, and. worked for a master plumber and painter, was found dead in a room at Messrs. J. Dennis and Company's copper works yesterday afternoon. Deceased, who is a married man, went to his work about noon, and, it is said, told his wife that he should probably be brought back upon a stretcher. It is said that his body presented every appear- ance of his having been poisoned. There were Superintendent Leab, 'tweeter Roche, four sergeants and twenty constables on Parade. The new clothing and the appointments of the men were carefully scrntin'zed by C donel Hamersley, with which he appeared to be sitisfied. The books were ex- amined and found in a correct and well kept condition. PRIZE FIGHT AT WIDNES.—It is stated that the police hive had it in contemplation to summon two men, named respectively Connor, of Alidwood-street, and Kelly, of Mile ton•road. to answer a charee of. committing a to each of the peace. It is said that on Friday afternoon they, along with a number of companions, proc. elect to a field in a seques- tered place in Crow Wood, where they engaged in a prize fight, and eight or nine rounds were gone through before the disgusting exhibition woe ',topped. A constable waiched the proceedings from a distance, while waiting for the arriyal,of some of his colleagues to asssist him in making arrests, but as they did not come he went forward, and took the names of the combatant,. As be approached the on- . lookers made a stampede. The stakes were £5 a side, and it appears that both men have Weil in training since Whit- son-week.

SINGULAR RECOVERY OF A LOST BANK NoTE.- - A£s Bank of England note which was lost in St. Helens on Saturday morning, was recovered under extraordinary circumstances. Mrs Seddon, of the Cotham Aims Hotel, near the Town Hall, sent her daughter Ada with £lO----a £5 note and £5 in gold —wrapped in a piece of newspaper, to the hone of Mr. Kerr, a mineral water manufacturer, in the neighbourhood. On the return of the girl with only .£5 in silver, it was ascertained that 111% Kerr had thrown the bank note into the street along with the piece of newspaper in Which it ' had been encloSed, as he was not aware of the presence of the bank note. A search failed to find the newspaper or the £5 note, and all hope of the recovery of the note was given up. However, on the return of Mrs Sed- don's servant, who had been on an errand to the market, she said she had picked up in Hardshaw- street a piece of paper bearing the words" Bank of England" which she took to be some tradesman's handbill. She placed it in her basket, and on reach- ing the hotel she threw it on the table with the goods she had purchased. On the " paper " being examined it was found to be the missing Bank of England note, much to the astonishment of the girl, who appeared totally ignorant of the value of , the "find. SIR R. A. CROSS AND Ti REPRESENTATION OF Sourn-WEst LANCASHIRE.—In consequence of the appointment of Sir Richard Assheton Cross to the office of Home Secretary, he will have to be re- elected for South-West Lancashire. It is believed that his election will be unopposed, the Liberals Of the division deeming it inexpedient to put the electors to the expense and trouble of a contest for the short period that will elapse prior to the general election. The new Home Secretary (Sir Richard Cross) in an addressAo the electors of South-West Lanaashire, soliciting a renewal during the few months that remain of the existing Parliament of the confidence which has existed so Jong, says : "If so honoured they may rely upon his doing everything in his power to • contribute to the main- tenanCe of peace abroad and the promotion of such securitytand general confidence as may tend to the revival of trade, and in home affairs to persevere in such legislation, as will tend to improve the so- cial and moral condition of large' masses of our fel- low-countrymen. The writ for a new election for South-West Lancashire, consequent on the accept- ance of office by Sir Richard Cross, was received on Thursday by Mr. James Williamson, the High Sheriff of the county, who has fixed Tuesday next for the day of nomination, and Tuesday, the 7th July, for the polling, should there be a contest. The place of nomination, as usual, will be St. George's Hall, Liverpool. Sir Richard Cross is n'ot expected to make any speech in the division before the nomi- nation day, when he will probably be in attendance and return thanks for his election. Coeormia. —Messrs. Lewis and Co. have com- menced running daily a coach and four between Manchester and Liverpool. The distance is covered in about four hours, changes of horses being made at Altrincham, Warrington, and Prescot. The service commenced on Tuesday, when the coach left Lewis's Liverpool establishment at nine o'clock. A number of bicyclists, attracted by the novelty, accompanied it on the way. Whilst proceeding between War- rington and Altrincham, a Liverpool rider of the name of Lucas, coming in contact with a stone, was pitched from his machine, alighting on his head, and sustaining injuries which rendered him insensible. The coach was stopped, and in it the injured man was taken to Altrincham, where he was left in a rather serious condition. Another bicyclist fell from his machine, but sustained no serious injury. The coach arrived at Manchester soon after two, having been delayed by these occurrences, and the return journey was commenced at 3-30 in the after- noon. At Warrington the coach stops at the Lion Hotel. On Tuesday also Hudson's coach made its first journey to Buxton, Mr. Hudson himself holding the reins. Sta Iting from Liverpool at 6-30 in the morning, Warrington was reached in a couple of hours. Here the party partook of breakfast at the Patten Arms Hotel. Luncheon was partaken of at Knutsford, and dinner at Macclesfield. The return journey was made yesterday. Both coaches passed through Prescot, and while the horses of Lewis's coach were being changed there, two of the fresh one. became restive, and considerably frightened some of the crowd who were watching. Finally one of them lay down in the road, and a start could not be made until another one was procured to take its place. IMPORTANT PROPERTY DISPUTE.—In the House of Lords, on Monday, their lordships resumed the further hearing of the appeal of William Horner, Blackburn, against a judgment of the Court of Ap- peal in an action as to the possession of the estate of Richard Harrison, of Warrington, who died in- testate in 1863. The appellant claims possession as the nearest heir, the other claimant being Mrs. Catherine Parker Slagg, wife of Mr. Slagg, M.P. The appellant got a judgment in his favour by Mr. Jus- tice Chitty, but the Court of Appeal reversed that order. It is only the real estate which is in question at the present time, the point in dispute having re- ference to the maternity of a John Harrison, an ancestor of the intestate, whether he was the son of John Harrison, formerly of Lea, near Preston, by his first wife, or his second wife, Arnie Harrison, formerly Anne Proctor. Mr. Homer claims through a sister of the grandmother of the intestate, and Mrs. Slagg through one of the three daughters of Anne Harrison by her first marriage, a question being raised as tb whether or not they were half- sisters of John Harrison, the intestate's ancestor.— Mr. lace, Q.C., for the respondent, Mrs. Slagg, con- tended that the appellant had not proved himself to be, and was not, in fact, the heir-at-law of Richard Harrison,the intestate, because it had been proved that John Harrison was the legitimate son of Anne Proctor by her second husband, John Harrison, of Lea, and because Mrs. Slagg was accordingly the heiress-at-law, or one of the co-heiresses-at-law of Richard Harrison, the intestate. The learned coun- sel submitted a photograph showing the signature of John Harrison obtained from various documents, contending that they showed that the father of the John Harrison who married Elizabeth Walrnsley was the same person as the son of John and Margerie Harrison and the same person as the individual who married Anne Proctor, so that by the aid of the signatures he submitted that Mrs:Slagg's relation- ship had been established as closer than that of Mr. ,Horner.—Mn M‘Naughten, Q.C., followed on the same side.—Mr. Field having replied for the appel- lant, their lordships intimated that they would probably dispose of the case on Thursday. On Fri- day the House of Lords gave judgment. The Master of the Rolls found for the appellant, and the Court of Appeal for Mrs.•Slagg. The House of Lords affirmed the latter judgment, dismissing the appeal with costs.

REPRESENTATION OF °MORTEN DIVISION.-011 Thursday morning, Mr. A. B. Forwood, leader of the Tory party in Liverpool, who has declined to con- test any of the Liverpool constituencies, agreed to come forward as the Conservative candidate for the Ormskirk division of South-West Lancashire at the general election. , COUNTY SESSIONS.—At the annual general session of Lancashire county magistrates held at Preston on Thursday an estimate was presented of the funds required by the treasurer to carry on the expendi- ture of the county to the end of February next. It showed an increase of £7,700 compared with the estimate of June, 1884. A report was also submitted showing a deficiency in the police superannuation fund to the amount of £5,227 upon the year, and a resolution was passed to defray the deficit out of the police rate of the county. THE VICAR OF EARLESTOWN SUMMONED.—A singular case, and one arising out of the recent Earlestown Church scandal, will be heard at the Newbon Petty Sessions to-day (Saturday). The Rev. T. R. Matthews, Vicar of St. John the Bap- tist's Church, has been summoned for "that you did counsel and procure one John Mahon to destroy certain vegetable productions, to wit, parsley, turnips, lettuces, &c., to the value of 15s. or there- abouts, the property of Walter Stacey, then grow- ing in a garden in his occupation. it will be remembered that Mr. Stacey was formerly the church cleaner and sexton, but he was one of the officers who received notice to leave during the general "clearing out" by the Vicar. The plants and vegetables which, it is alleged, were recently destroyed by the orders of the Vicar, were grow- ing on the plot of land adjoining the schoolroom in Market-street. The land belongs to the trustees of the school, and about 18 years ago the Rev. Canon Whitley, Rector of Wargrave, gave Mr. Stacey permission to use the land for any garden- ing purposes until it was required for the erection of an additional school, or an extension of the present school premises. Since' then Mr. Stacey has been in undisputed possession of a portion of the ground, while Mr. James Sharpe and the Rev. T. R. Matthews— who came some years later— have also cultivated other portions. Dur- ing the last few months, however, it is stated that the Vicar has manifested a desire to turn Mr. Stacey away from the garden, and as Mr. Stacey refused to leave at his bidding, as he contended the Vicar had no authority to order him away, the Vicar --as alleged 'by the summo:-..5---gave orders for all the growing vegetables in Mr. Stacey's plot to be destroyed. The soil has been completely over- turned, and lettuces, cabbages, parsley, and other vegetable's which were growing in abundance were uprooted and rendered valueless. Hence the pre- sent legal proceedings, which have occasioned a lively interest in the neighbourhood. It may be added that some months ago Mrs. Stacey brought a county court action against the Rev. T. R. Matthews for the recovery of a sum of money alleged to be due for washing. RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY. BEER OR MONEY.—MIS Rop4S, the nurse recently ap- pointed by the Board, wrote asking that she might receive her salary monthly instead of quarterly, and also that she should receive money instead of an allowance of leer. Is was decided to make no change in the time of payment, and la discussion ensued regarding the second r,quest. Some members were of opinion that Mrs Rogers should have an I equivalent to the beer allowance in money, while others I maintained that as the beer was adowed she should use it or I not, as she liked, but should not have a money equivalent if She did not care for the beer. A resolution that she be allowed the money, and an amendment to the negative were proposed. Mr. Wilsey remarked that it was considered the better plan for it to be optional on the part of officer sof workhouses whether they had beer or money, and, on a vote being taken, it was d‘cided by a large majorify that Mrs Rogers be allowed to have a money allowance. - - THE BIRTH AND DEATH RATE OF Winiustorost. —For week ending Saturday, June 20th, 1885.—The mean temperature was 578 Fahr. and therefore 3.8 degrees higher than the preceding week. The ' maximum temperature 71 Fahrenheit, was recorded on the 14th inst., and the minimum temperature, 48 Fahrenheit, on the 17th inst. The rainfall measured .59in. The general direction of the wind was W. During the week, which was the 25th of the current year, 34 births land /7 deaths were registered. The death rate from all causes was equal to 19.4 per 1,000, against 15.1 the average of the previou.s four weeks, and against 26.1 the cor- responding week of last year. The deaths included 1 from whooping cough, 1 from rheumatic fever, 4 from tubercular diseases, 2 from oldage, 5 from brain disease, and 3 from lung disease. WO 08.908 of scarlatina, 3 of measles, and one of whooping Gough were reported under the requirements of the Act of Parliament.—JouN. IL Gonztarx, Medical. Officer of Health.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. MoNDAT.—Before Alderman Holmes, Councillor Greening,

and Mr. John Pairciough. MISCELLANiOUS.—The following cases of drunkenness were dealt with :—Jesse Parr, in Orford-avenue, on the pre- vious day, fined 23 6d, including costs; Edward Griffin. jun., in Winwick-street, on the 31st May, and in Golden Grove-street, on the 13th June, fined 15s and costs; Edward Crosby, in Golden Grove-street, on the 13th inst., fined 103 and costs; John Connelley, in Buttermarket-street, on the 14th inst., fined 5s and costs; Robert Dakin, in Bridge-street, on the 13th inst., sent to prison for a month.—Bridget White, charged with committing a breach of the peace by assaulting Mary McHugh, at Bakehouse-yard, on the 3rd Inst., was ordered to find a surety for her good behaviour.— Mary Dolan, for committing a breach of the peace in , Orford-lane, on the 11th inst., was ordered to be bound over to keep the peace for six months.—Charles Stuart, for allowing a horse to stray in Stamford-street, on the 13th inst., was fined 23 61 and costs.—Gilbert Warburton, charged with keeping a hand cart standing an unreasonable time in Market-street, on the 14th inst., was dismissed, he having been ignorant of the bye-laws. TUESDAY.—Before Messrs. C. Breadbent and E. J. Guest. A DRUNKEN Dravart.—Arthur Millwood was charged with having been drunk whilst in charge or a 'bus on the previous day, in Bridge-street, and was fined 53, including costs. .
WEDNESDAY.—Before Alderman Cbandley.

Mr. Browne de- fended.--Anu Kenwick was charged with using threats to Margaret Messenger on the 19th inst. Mr. A. Browne de- fended.—The case was dismissed.

Joseph Basnett, Cather- ine Holleran, Cicely Riley. Timothy Mitchell, Albert Young. Several witnesses were called,, and the Bench, coming to the conclusion that the parties had been con- cerned in a disgraceful row, ordettd them both to be bound oyer to keep the peace.

div.head: CYCLISTS FROM ST. HELENS.
div.p: CYCLISTS FROM ST. HELENS.

[BY TRAVELLER.] The other day I dropped in with a party of jolly roving cyclists from St. Helens. They were on their way home after an enjoyable "spin" to Lymm, and from their lively and interesting con- versation I gathered they had had a most enjoyable " ramble." When Warrington was reached on the return journey darkness and a heavy downpour of rain compelled them to leave the "road" for the "rail," and by that means my lot was cast amongst them. It is needless to add their conversation was most interesting, and, to a certain degree, instruc- tive, while hearty peals of laughter were frequent. As could only be expected, talk was principally con- fined to " wheeldom," incidents and experiences in connection with which were narrated. For instance, the recent feat of bicytle-ridink from John O'Groats to Lands End was eagerly discussed—a discussion Which evidenced an extraordinary degree of ignorance, or rather forgetfulness, to which I my- self must also plead guilty. One of the party hap- pened to ask, "What was the distance travelled ? to which " a friend replied, "Somewhere between 300 and 400 miles." Another individual laughingly said it was nearer 900 miles; while a third declared "England is 395 miles in length." The hilly coun- try beyond Carlile was briefly touched upon, and an allusion to the "hot work" for bicyclists among the Highlands drew forth the observation that the best " clothing " for "men of the wheel" in that part of the world was a pair of bathing drawers. This naturally suggested to one's mind the familiar Scotch " kilties," and the idea evidently struck one menTher, for he created great amusement by his ob- servation that he had recently seen in St. Helens a tall man wearing " kilties" whose legs were so thin they would scarcely throw a shadow. From " kil- ties " the conversation went on to" bag-pipes," and one cyclist narrated a friend's experience, where, he said, there were four pipers in a small room "only about two yards square." Each played a dif- ferent tune to his fellow, and the speakers' friend, immensely fond of the "b-pipes," said, "The music was delightful, and we did enjoy ourselves." Laughter greeted this re- mark, amid which ore person, with a significant wink, observed that if he had been in that trying situation'he should have been anxious to insert the point of 8 pin in a vital part of the "wind-bags."

The talk was here interrupted by the stoppage of the train at a station wyse name, judging by the shouts of the railway officials, was "S'Noak." The name of this station,' said one, "I could not under- stand when first I came this way;" a remark which was endorsed by everyone present as their own ex- perience. Allusions to the mystifying shouts of railway officials in general followed-, Cieckheaton, in Yorkshire, being particularly instanced. Here, it was said, a big burly rough-voiced Yorkshireman walked along the train calling in drawling accents " Cleckheaton," while behind would be a little, quick and shrill-voiced Cockney, whose rapid pro- nunciations of "Clecketon" reminded the passen- gers of a little bantam cock. From the calls of officials their appearance, dress, and manners next cropped up for discussion, and an individual inter- ested the company by his graphic description of the abnormally large size of the boots worn by one of the porters at a station in the North. It being de- clared that the official in question had come from abroad, "I am sure," said the narrator, "he must have come in one of his boots or boats, and used the other as a cabin for first-class passengers." The ' closing subject was the vagaries of the weather, and an amusing "fact" was explained. One of the cyclists visiting a friend during the recent hot weather found him sitting on a warm pipe in the greenhouse.- On asking his friend why he had taken his seat there, the reply was, "I am only training for a warming shop." This was a fitting termina- tion to the pleasant few minutes I had spent among my friends. Their genuinely humourous conversa- tion, entirely free from vulgarity or anything ob- jectionable, greatly enlivened what would otherwise lave been a monotonous railway journey.

div.head: LIBERAL MEETINGS IN CHESHIRE.
div.p: LIBERAL MEETINGS IN CHESHIRE.

Meetings in support of the candidature of Mr. I. S. Lead.= for the Altrincham Parliamentary Division were held at Lynam and Heatley on Saturday evening, and were well at- tended, considerable erathueiascri being manifested. The first was held near the Jolly Thrasher Inn, Broom Edge, Lymm, whence the candidate and some of his friends drove to Heatley, where the second was hell. Mr. T. W. Killick, chairman of the Executive Committee, presided at both meetings, and spoke ably in support of Mr. Leadam and his cause. There were also present a number of local gentle- men and others interested in Libzralism, these including, at Lymm, Messrs. McKay, Brewtnall, and W. Milne; and at Heatley, Messrs. Milne, Brewtnall, Swanwick, Dutton, Stelfox. Mr. LEADASI, speaking at Lymm, was received with cheers. He said that he proposed to confine his remarks to topics that wculd be of especial interest to his auditors, who were chiefly employed in agriculture. His Tory friends seemed to think it presumption on his part to address an audience on that subject. and the secretary to the Conservative Associa- tion had said that he (Mr. Leadam) did not know much about agricultural questions. Unfortunately, however, that gentleman had not been to the trouble of enquirine into the matter, or be would have found that he was well acquainted with the principal needs of the farmers. (Hear, hear.) The great difficulty that the farmer in in my parts of the coun- try met with was to find labour, and on the other hand, the difficulty to find employment was met with by the agricul- tural labourer. What he (the speaker) had for years past advocated was a system of reforms, the effect of which I would be to enable the farmer to give a greater amount of employment to the labourer, and to keep the labourer em- ployed upon the land in a condition more pros- perous than he had hitherto enjoyed. He was happy to note that there was a movement amongst Cheshire men, which he was prepared to welcome. The general election of 1880 was marked by a great defec- tion of farmers from the Conservative party ; after six years of Tory administration the farmers became aware that they had nothing to expect from that party. He congratulated himself, therefore, especially upon that movement of the Cheshire farmers for this reason. It was true lee was a candidate seeking the suffrages of the farmers, but he was in a strong position. Instead of having to run after the farmers in Quest of their votes, the farmers came to him, and were beginning to embrace the views which for years he had advanced. (Applause.) What were the principal burdens under which the farmer laboured? The first was rent. (Hear, hear.) Durieg the past 25 years rents had increased at a most remarkable rate. The capital value of the land had increased since 18534 by £380,000,000, and of that sum, according to an authority upon the subject— Sir James Caird—not more than £60,000,000 was due to landlords' improvements. That meant that £320,000,000 of this increased rental, after allowing for sufficient increment, had come out of the pockets of the tenant farmer. In that district, he was told, there was no objection to the system, ' because farmers were so prosperous and landlords so good ' that injustice was never committed. He did not charge the landlords with any injustice, because as a body they were honourable men. The object of legislation, however, was not to restrain the good, but the evil. (Hear, hear.) Laws were not made to keep the good but the evil in order. (Ap- plause.) Agriculture was greatly depressed, although rents had risen to so great an extent. Tenant farmers could not now exist, and were in many cases quitting their farms, Tenant farmers, on leaving their holdings, received nothing ' from their landlords for the improvements they had effected, which, be maintained, was an injustice. It was unjust nit I only to the individual tenants, but also to the nation, as it checked the industry of the tenant farmers, who put as little Into the soil as they possibly could. What was in regard to this matter the att,tude of the Conservative party? They ' must watch what the leaders of that party had to say about it. He found that when Conservative candidates referred to it, they made numerous prowises. Conservative candi- dates, however, would not dictaTla the action of the party to which they belonged. His opponent, Mr. John Brooke, would not dictate that action, but would follow the lead of Lord Salisbury, Mr. Chaplin, and others. Lord Salisbury had distinctly announced in a reCent speech the line the Conservative party intended to take on the questions that were being raised in the interests of the tenant farmers. Lord Salisbury admitted that increased protection for the farmer was an excellent thine, " but," he said, "it was not so important as the undisturbed continuance of arrange- ments which have existed for a vast number of years." (Laughter.) Referring to an amendment brought in by Sir t Michael-Hicks Beach, the effect of which was that Where a I farmer had to quit his holding he should be robbed of half I the compensation due to him on the gronnd that part of the improvement was due to the "inherent capabili- ties of the soil," Mr. Leadam said that was an injustice, because for what did the farmer pay rent but for the "inherent capability of the soil P" The Conservatives opposed the proposal to make that clause of the Agricultural Holdings Act retrospective in cases where the farmer had effected improvements before it was passed, and they had voted prejudicially to the farmer's in- terests again on the question of notice to quit. (Hear hear.) Then there was the law of distress, the aceion of which, in the first place had been to send up rents, Imam the land- lord in prosperous times had attempted, and the land agent had even more ettemoted, to select that tenant velao would make the bees offer, irrespective very biten of Whether he weenld be able to carry out the ffers he had made, (Hear, hear.) His opinion wee that the law of dise tress Should be altogether abolished. Respecting the Votes of the Cheshire county members, he found that In the present Parliament there had been 14 divisions on agricul- tural questions. In three of these Mr. Warburton had voted against the tenants' Interest, and he had been absent on 11 divisions. Those were the services which he supposed Mr. Warburton lead been elected to render to the farmers. Then again, Mr. Egerton had been absent on eight divisions, and had voted against the tenants: interest on six divisions, so that he had done twice as much injury as Mr. Warbur- ton. (Laughter.) Mr. W. Cunliffe Brooks, the uncle ef Mr. John Brooks, was absent on every single division, and that was the way in which he served the farmers. (Renewed laughter.) Mr. W. J. Legh was present in four divisions, when he voted against the farmers' interest. The adherence of the farmers to Conservative principles had now, however, been shattered, and he hoped at the next general election it would be broken for ever. (Hear hear, and applause.) Upon the rate question it should be remembered that the Liberal policy was to divide the hurthen of rates equally between the landlord and the tenant. It was a just proposal that the man whom the ratea permanently benefited, the owner of the soil, should pay half of them, and that was what the Liberal party were endeavouring to obtain for the farmer. The in- creased tax upon spirits was a very fair tax, because if poor men were taxed it could not be put upon anything better than upon ardent spirits. (Hear, hear.) The Conserva- tive proposal, it must not be forgotten, was to tax tea, bread, clothing, and other necessaries of life. The Conserva- tives had but one object in view, and that was to maintain the present position of the landed interest, and they were not willing to grant a system of representative government. It might be said that he appealed to class interests, but if he did it was because he believed class interests in those matters were national interests. (Applause). At Heatley Mr. Leadam referred to statements made by Mr. Brooks, which, he said, had only to be pricked with fact and the bubble burst. 'rho people of this country, he proceeded, would next November have to choose between a government of re-action and one of progress, a government which would do nothing to relieve farmers' interests, and one which lead sheen its desire to help both farmer and farm labourer. They would have to choose, whether the whole of the taxes of the country should be raised from the working-classee, or make the landed interest pay its fair proportien. (Applause.) At born meetings resolutions were passed declaring Mr. Leadam a fit and proper person to represent that division in Parliament.

BIRCH V. LATCHFORD.—PIayed at Latchford on Satnre day. Score :—Latchford, 24 ; Birch, 29. BRICVSTREET AND BRIAR'S-GREEN SUNDAE SCHOOLS.— I MARRIED V. SINGLE.—This match was played on Walking Day, and resulten ia an easy Victory for the single team by 37 runs. .1. James. W. Critcbley, and J. Critchley each batted well for the latter team. Score :—Single, 54; Mar- ried, 17. WARRINOTON V. NEWTON.—Warrington took a SOME- what weak team to Newton, on Saturday, but succeeded in winning by 93 runs. Fairclough won the toss and put Aewten in to the bowling of the brothers Lawton. Armstrong took Dudgeon behind the wicket, and Lane grion after hit his wicket, and H. Jolley now came off with a fast low catch at point from Parks, and J. C. Lawton secured Latchford at slip. Longton was playing steadily, and runs came very slowly. Hindley tried hard bitting, but was caught at his first attempt by Clarke holding a very high hit to the long field. At 30 Longton was taken by Jolley running in from point. Clarke bowled the next comer before he scared, and Fairclough came in. He began scoring at once, and kept the field alive by attempts to ran. Slater hit freely and put one in the road for four, but was taken in the slips. Stone was taken first ball by Armstrong. Jolley was applauded at this time for saving two smart cats, and Hind was changed for Clarke. From Htskell's second over, he put , one behind cover, to which Clarke got back, and the innings I closed for 57. Warrington began with Fairclough and T. Jolley, and 18 were scored when Fairclough was ran out from a smart throw in by Lane- Jolley was caught at mid- off, and C. G. Lawton and Clarke were partners. The latter was bowled off his pads, and J. C. Lawton partnered his brother. A long stand was made; 51 runs were put on, of which the last comer scored 30 and was run out similarly to Fairclough. Armstrong played carefully, but was caught from a high return. Hind played a ball, and in trying to save it trout his wickets he hushed it in. The match at Manchester between Lancashire and York- shire terminated on Saturday, the result being :—Lanca- shire, 168 and 138; Yorkshire, 158 and 75. The ground was in poor condition in consequence of the rain, which militated against good crickst.—As was very generally ex- pected, the task Surrey had set Cambridge for Saturday proved far too heavy for the Light Blues, and early in the afternoon ths match ended in favour of Surrey by 131 run. Art hour und a hales pia 'Y at Brighton on Wednesday' brought the match between Sussex and Lancashire to a conclusion, Lancashire winning a well-contested game by 33 runs. The result was in accord with general expecta. tion, as it was thought the task set before Sussex of malt. ing 103 runs for their last five wickets was too heavy. Jesse Hide was soon out, the sixth wicket falling at Mr. Wyatt then joined Quaife, and th 9 untAtter bitting freely and well 35 runs were added bottle Quaife had to leave. Latterly Mr. Wyatt could a no assistance, and shortly after one o'clock the Sattex innings closed for 143 Mr. Wyatt carried out his bat for 36, made up of seven 4's, , a three, and five singles. Barlow had a capital analysis, and Watson bo eried very steadily. The weather was fine, and the att.P.mdanee fairly good. little over an hour's play on Wednesday was sufficient , 'co finish off the match M.C.C. and Ground v. Cambridge University at Lord's Ground, London the M.C.C. gaining an easy victory over Cambridge University by eight wickets. The M.C.C. had been left with 97 to get to win, and of this number 13 had been made without the loss of a wicket. On Wednesday morning the result was soon put beyond doubt by the brilliant batting of Mr. G. B. Studd, in whose not-out innings of 59 were nine 4's, two 3's, and three 2's. _ . .

A meeting, of the Managing Committee of the Kent County Cricket Club was held on Monday at the Golden Cross Hotel, Charing-cross. The question respecting un- fair bowling, at issue between Kent and Lancashire, was discussed at the meeting, and it was decided to send the following letter to the Lancaster County Cricket Club:— . am directed by the Managing Committee of the Kent County Cricket Club to inforun you that, haying every confidence in the judgment and impartiality of the gentle- men who have played and do play for the County Eleven, and haying been informed by them that your club is in the habit of employing bowlers whose action is net consistently fair, the Committee has decided to decline to play a return match with your club this year. The Committee will be glad to know whether you would prefer to claim the match by default without appearance on the ground, or to adopt the alternative course suggested by Lord Harris in his let- ter.--I am, &C., Anruure J. LANCASTER, Secretary (pro tern.)—To S. H. Swire, Esq., Hon Secretary, the Lancaster County and Manchester Cricket Club."

A Purclu BICYCLE RIDE.—A notable ride has just b2en accomplished by Mr. H. W. Cooper, a member of the Liver- pool Prince's -B.C. He has reached London by way of Coventry, a distance of 210 miles, in a few minutes less than 24 hours, including stoppiges for refreshments extending to an hour and a half.

An attempt has been made in some quarters to cast odium on Earl Spencer for his 'stealthy" departure from Dublin Last week. His Lordship has written a letter to Sir Bernard Burke showing that his unexpected i•mrney across Channel was a matter of necessity, and asking him to make arrange- ments for a " reception " to be held in Duhlin next Saturday by himself and Countess Spencer. THE SKYE CROFTERS.—In accordance with instructions from the Admiralty, the marines who had been stationed for some time in Skye left on Wednesday for Inverness, en route to Portsmouth. They were heartily cheered as they left the Nand, where their behaviour has been very exemplary. All the extra policemen who were on special service in Skye have also returned to their own respective stations. AN 'rasa TEAGEDY.—On Tuesday, at Garvagh, the bodies cf a farmer named Killough and his wife were inter- red in one grave. The man was found hanging from a beam in his barn, and in the room his wife was discovered dead on a bed, her bead being dreadfully cut, and her face so mutilated by wounds as to be almost unrecognisable. A woman named Millar was also found covered with wounds, and her death is hourly expected. Ki lough had mur- dered his wife; being interrupted by the woman Millar, be attacked her and left her for dead; and then hanged himself.
