THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, • JUNE 27 1885. THE PENDLEBURY COLLIERY TIXPLOSION. The number of deaths by the terrible explosion at Clifton Hall Colliery, Pendlebury, is over 170. On Saturday night, after the exploring parties were withdrawn, a successful attempt was made to light the furnace at the bottom of the upcast shaft with a view to improve the ventilation. Ano- ther good effect was produced by the lighting of the fire. The iron bands round the shaft had contracted with the cold, and water in large quantities was pouring into the shaft and running int, the works. The heat expanded the bands, and the flow of water was stopped. After this the explorers were able to recommence their labours, and during the night and Sunday they Bent up 30 bodies. Nearly the whole of these were recognised. Mr. Price opened the inquest on Saturday morning. The operation of viewing the bodies occupied nearly two hohre, and in the court-room, which was at the Mechanics' Insti- tute, Pendlebury, the proceedings were of a formal charac- ter. The evidence was confined exclusively to the iden- tification of the bodies, and, an order for burial having been given in each case, tbe inquiry was adjourned until next Tuesday. A meetieg convened by the Mayor of Manchester was, on Saturday, held in the Mayor's parlour of the Town Hall, to consider what steps could be taken to relieve the victims of the disaster. A subscription list was opened, and a sub-! , stantial amount was immediately contributed. It was an- nounced that collections were to be made in all co-operative stores and many churches and chapels. A resolution was passed expressing the heart-felt sympathy of the meeting with the widows and orphans and other relatives of the vic- tims of the disaster, and appointing an influential committee to concert measures of relief. A further resolution accepted the co-operation of the Mayor of London, and thanked him for his sympathy. Messrs. Knowles and Son, the proprie- tors of the colliery, have given to each family £1 103. to as- sist in the purchase of coffins. £10,400 will be paid from the colliery insurance fund to the families of the killed. Each widow will be paid 5s per week for two years, and each child 2s 6d per week until it is 10 years of age. £15,000 is required to be raised by subscriptions. I Nearly 40 bodies of the ill-fated miners were interred on Sunday. The village of Pendlebury, claiming by far the larger number of the people employed at the colliery as residents' proved a great centre of attraction to visitors, and thousands flocked to the parish until long before three o'clock, the hour at which the sad ceremonies commenced, the main street was crowded with arrivals. .At Clifton, also, where some eight funerals took place, there was a numerous attendance of visitors, and a similar state of things is repor- ted both of Swinton and Irlama-o'-th'-Heights. The scene at Christ Church, Pendlebury, was extremely impressive. No one was allowed to pass into the precincts of the burial ground, but relatives or friends of the unfortu- nate men or those who were connected with the funerals. Admirable order was maintained, and as each cortege arrived the spectators stood aside and many reverentially raised their hats as the mourners, preceded by the coffins, walked up the short avenue to the church. Many expres- sions of sympathy were heard, and there were not a few who betrayed emotions by shedding tears, as the remains of their acquaintances were removed to their last resting places. Most of the principal mourners were the widows of the un- fortunate men, and as they were led up to the church and afterwards to the grave side by brothers or brothers-in-law, that anguish was of a kind most painful to witness. Two more deaths have resulted from the recent explosion, and on Wednesday three more bodies were recovered, mak- ing the total ascertained number .f deaths 176. The col- liery officials believe that all the killed have now been got out, but in other quarters it is supposed that there are still two or three more in the workings. The bodies found on Wednesday were those of two cffiliers named Hughes and Evans, and that of the furnaceman, Thomas Taylor. The latter had been driven 40 yards along a return airway by the force of the explosion, and all three were very badly burned. In the case of a man named Slattery a somewhat singular dispute has arisen. A body was identified on Mon- day by a man named Gavin as that of Thomas Slattery. That body was afterwards buried in that name. Now, how- ever, some twenty of Slatterv's neighbours and fellow- workmen say that the body identified by Gavin was not Slattery at all, and they state that a body which had note before been recognised was Slattery's. The deceased man's wife, however, says that this body is not her husband's, and on Wednesday it was interred as that of a man unknown.

div.head: ANOTHER EXPLOSION.-NINE LIVES LOST.
div.p: ANOTHER EXPLOSION.-NINE LIVES LOST.

An explosion occurred at the Barley Pit of the Apedale Collieries, owned by Messrs. Sainer and Company, at Ape- dale, near Newcastle-under-Lyne, on Saturday morning, by which nine lives were lost. The pit lies about midway be- tween the colliery villages of Silverdale and Chesterton, and employs about 200 men and boys. At six o'clock on Saturday morning the men descended to their work, the workings having previously been examined and reported clear of gas and all right. The ventilation of the mine is on the most approved principle, and it is said to be one of best managed collieries in the district. On Saturday morn- ing 192 men went to work and all seemed right until a little after nine o'clock, when a terrific explosion occurred, the report of which was heard for a considerable distance. 'A soon as an exploring party could be got together, and a descent was made, it was discovered that the explosion bad taken place in what is known as the south ten-foot seam, which is a new working being opened out, where 12 men only were employed. The explosion seemed to have taken piece at the heading, where probably a shot had been fired. Immediately the nature of the occurrence became known, Mr. J. Cadman, the certificated manager, and Mr. Thomas Bulme. the overlooker, who were on the bank at the time, descended the shaft, and other exploring parties were organised for the purpose of relief. When it was dis- covered that the disaster had been confined to the particular spot where the explosion had occurred, the men were as hastily as possible sent up the pit from the other seams of the mine. The exploring parties found the ventilation somewhat deranged and the roadways injured, and as quickly as possible the ventilation was restored. Mr. Cad- man and several of the explorers were overcome with after. damp, and had to be treated by medical men, who by this time had been sent for. The afterdamp and several falls considerably retarded explorations, and it was not until after two o'clock that the first body was sent to the surface. Several others were recovered daring tde afternoon, but the whole were not got out of the workings until Tuesday. Iden- tification of the bodies was very difilcult, all being mutilated in a horrible manner. An inquest on the bodies of the de- paged was formally opened on Tuesday,

div.head: 'SOUTH-WEST LANCASHIRE POLLING
div.p: 'SOUTH-WEST LANCASHIRE POLLING
DISTRIC rs. SUGGESTED ALTERATIONS.

A meeting of the Sub-Committee of the JusticeS Of the county, appointed at the last General Sessions, was held on Monday, at Liverpool, to consider what alteration of polling districts should be recommended for the approval of the General Sessions next month. Mr. U. H. Croxden Powell represented the Liberals, and Mr. W. Woodnorth the Con- servatives. The recommendations for the various divisions of the county included the following : ORMSICIRK DIVISION, " B."—Polling places have been established as follows for this division :—Burscough—for the townships of Burscough and Latham ; Kirkby—for Kirkby and Simonswood ; Maghull—for Aintree, Lunt, Lydiate, Maghull, Melling, Netherton, and Set ton; Orms- kirk—for Aughton, Bickerstaffe, and Ormskirk ; Cobol- land—for Dalton and Upholland ' • Prescot—for Croxteth Park, Knowsley, and Prescot ; Scarisbrick Bridge—fir Scarisbrick, Haleall, and Downholland ; Seaforth—for Lith- erland, Orrell, and Ford; Skelmersdale—for the township of kelmersdale.

WIDNES DIVISION. "D."—ln this division, Garston will be the polling place for the townships of Allerton, Garston, and Speke ; Halewood for Hale and Halewood townships; fluyton for Huvton-with-Robv, Tarhock, and Whiston ; and Much Woolton for Much and Little Woolton. In the case of Widnes some discussion arose. Mr. Powell said a depu- tation was in attendance wishful to explain the views of Widnes en the subject of polling places. He explained the views of the deputation, who were than invited to attend the committee. Mr. E. Carey and Mr. H. B. Shores then entered the room, and stated their case, ill ustratibg their views by reference to certain districts on the map. After the deputation had withdrawn, considerable discussion took place, and the claim of three districts for Widnes was not accepted. Mr. Powell urged the committee to consider a suggestion he would make that two districts might be formed to meet the public convenience of the three town- ships. This the committee agreed to after some further dis- cussion, so that the old polling district will be now divided into two districts :—Widnes South, being the portion of the township south of the London and North-Western Com- pany's low level railway, with a polling place at or near the West-street schools; and Widnes North, which will contain so much of the townships as is north of the said railway, to- gether with the townships of Ditton and Cronton, with a polling centre about Simm's Cross.

• NEWTON DIVISION, "E."—The townships of Ashton-in. Makerfield, Idaydock, Golborne, Rainhjll, Raiford, and Rixton-with-Glazebrook are each made into separate polling districts. Winwick is the polling place for Burtonwood, Houghton, Middleton and Arbury, southworth-with-Croft, and Winwick-with-Hulme. 'The electors in the township of Newton will vote at Earlestown. The townships of Bit- liege Chapel-end and Billinge Higher-end, with the town- ship of Winstanley will vote at Billinge Chapel-end. The freeholders of St. Helens and the electors of the extra-muni- cipal townships of Eccle-ton and Windle will vote at St. Helens. '1 he townships of Poalton-with-Fearnhead, War- rington, and Woolston-with-Mariinscroft will vote at War- rington. The townships of Bold, Cuerdley, Great Sankey, aud Penketh at Great Sankey. LEIGH DIVISION, " G."—ln this district little alteration is recommended for the present year. The polling places for Atherton is in the township, Culcheth township at Cul- cheth, Lowton for K:nyon and Lowfon, Leigh for Bedford, Pennington, and West Leigh, and at Tyldssley for Astley and Tyldesley. . . .

The remaining divisi,ms in which alterations were sug- gested were ,:outhport Division, "A;" Bootle Division," C;' and Ince Division, "F." It is suggested that several of the more populous districts iniy have to be altered next year, but owing to the brief space of time allowed by the Acts for the construction of sep irate lists the.overseers cannot have the work completed for a dissolution in the month of No- vem her;
Wednesday was the second day of the Handel Fes- tival at the Crystal Palace. The number of visitors was 22,161.

div.head: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
div.p: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
--- HOUSE OF LORDS.—TURSDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at 4-15.

There was a large attendance of Peers, especially on the Opposition benches, which were still occupied by the Con- servative party. In the Peeresses Galleries almost every seat was occupied. Amongst those present on the Minis- terial side were the Archbishop of York, the Bishops of Car- lisle. Winchester, Lichfield, and Gloucester, and Bristol; Earl Spencer, the Earl of Derby, the Earl of Kimberley, the Earl of Rosebery, the Earl of Northbrook, Lord Carlingford, Lord Sudeley. the Duke of Argyll, the Marquis of Ripen, Lord Sherbrook, and Lord Monk Bretton. fin the Opposi- tum side were the Duke of Richmond and Lord Cranbrook, the Earl of Latham, Earl of Galloway, Lord Ellenborough, Earl Stanhope, and Lord Norton. The Prince of Wales en- tered the Rouse at half-past four, and took his usual seat on the cross benches. Earl Granville, who came in shortly be- fore the half hour, made his way to the Front Opposition benches and sat there for a few minutes between the Duke of Richmond and Lerd Cranbrook, with both of whom he carried on an earnest conversation. On leaving them he crossed over to his customary place, and immediately after- wards rose to make the expected statement with:regard to the Ministerial crisis.

LORD SALISBURY AT WINDSOR.—EarI GRANVILLE said: I am authorised to state that Lord Salisbury has gone down to Windsor and has accepted office, and at his desire I shall propose, when the proceedings of to-day close, the adjourn- ment of the House as usual till Thursday. (Laughter.) MisonLaraotis.—Some private bills were advanced a stage.--Lord WENLOCK moved for the second reading of the Yorkshire Registration Bill which, he explained, bad been introduced at the instigation of Yorkshire bankers whose interests were prejudiced by the act passed in 1884, I and the object was to amend that Act. The Bill was read a second time.—The Burial Boards (Contested Elections) Bill was read a third time and passed. THE ,REDISTRIBUTION BILL PASSED.

On the consideration of the Commons' reasons for dis- agreeing to some of the Lords' amendments to the Parlia- mentary Elections (Redistribution) Bill. Lord PENMAN moved that the reasons should be considered that day six months.—The amendment was put and negatived. The Earl of KIMBERLEY proposed that their Lordships should not insist upon their amendment relating to Jed- burgh.—The Marquis of LOTHIAN, as the mover of the amendment with which the Commons disagreed, expressed surprise at the view taken in the other House, as Jedburgh was not, as had been stated, closely connected with the county, and was homogeneous with the border burghs. His object was that the vote of the agricultural labourer should receive its full value, and the description which Mr. Ire- velyan gave of his amendment was most objectionable and of a party character, applied to the proposal made in the bill as it was sent up to their Lordships. He felt so strongly on the subject that he was inclined to ask their Lordships to adhere to their amendment.—Lord Crux- BROOK stated that he voted with the noble Marquis on the previous occasion, but as the amendment was not supported by the leaders on either side in the House of Commons, and having regard to present circumstances, he advised that it should not be pressed.—The Earl of MORTON took the same view.—The Earl of GALLOWAY really hoped the noble Mar- quis would not pet the House to the trouble of dividing. He was connected with a group of boroughs that would be disfranchised by the bill, and be had great objection to it ; but after it was publicly announced that the leaders on the two sides had determined upon the principal features of .the bill, he felt it would not be right to raise any objection to it.—The Earl of HARROWBY urged that it would be very undesirable at that moment to introduce complications be- tween the two Houses, and, giving the noble Marquis every credit for the sincerity of his motives, he hoped he would withdraw his opposition.—The Marquis of LOTHIAN said he would not further press his objection, and the amendment wa4 not insisted upon.—The Earl of KIMBERLEY then moved that the House should not insist upon its ether amendment, substituting Burstal for Spen Valley.—The Earl of FAVERSHAM proposed that their Lordships should adhere to their decision.—The Earl of KIMBERLEY pressed ' upon their Lordships the inconven,ence of delaying the passing of the bill; and Lord CRANBROOK, though with reluctance, advised Lord Faversham not to press his amend- ment, which was not insisted upon. WOMEN'S SHFFRAGE.—Lord PENMAN rose, in a full House, to move the second reading of the Women's Suffrage Bill, but Peers immediately began to leave in large num- bers, and before the noble lord had concluded the few sen- tences in which he recommended the measure to the House, he had but a scanty audience.—The Earl of ROSEBERY

could not consider that a decorous or proper manner of raising the question. He could not give his vote on a matter of such importance without expressing his views upon it, and he for one should leave the liouse.—The Earl of KIMBERLEY would vote against the bill without any refer- ence to its merits, but merely on the ground that he did not think that a praper time to raise the question.—On a division being challenged, the Earl of Rosebery left the House, and Earl Granville, Lord Barrington, the Marquis of Lothian, and several other peers went within' the rails of the Throne to avoid recording their votes.—The bill was thrown out by 36 votes to 8.
TRH CROFT.' ERS' CO MIIISSION.—Lord ETTERICK COM•

plained of the statement made by the Duke of Argyll on May 7th that a letter from him to the Crofters' Commission had been. impressed. The matter, he said, was carefully considered by the Commissioners, wno decided that it should not be published with their report. Tae noble Mike bad himself secured the publication of the letter all over Scot- land. —The Duke of ARGYLL said that amongst a great deal of good evidence, the Commissioners received a great deal of evidence that was utter rubbish, Crofters who went before them being primed in the statements that they were to make. He contended that he had a perfect right to direct the attention of the public and of the Commissioners to the true state of the facts, and that hia letter ought to have been included in their report. Their Lordships adjourned at 5.35 till Thursday. HOUSE OF CONlMONS.—Tussney.

The Spealt-eiio-oklhe-cl:ai-r-;r4 0, at which hour there were very few members in the House, though a fair sprink- ling could be seen through the lobby doorway. During the interval up to half-past four, however, members continued to arrive, and when the hour for commencing business had come the House had begun to assume an animated appear- ance, most of the benches on both sides Being filled, while the Strangers' Galleries were also full of expectant occu- pants. Just before the half-hour, the entrance of Mr. Gladstone from behind the Speaker's chair was greeted with a cordial cheer from the Liberal benches. Parties not hav- ing as yet changed sides, the right hon. gentleman took his usual seat with his colleagues on the Treasury bench. The' only occupants of the front Opposition bench were the two Conservative whips—Sir William Hart Dyke and Mr. H. Rowland Winn. When the notices of motion were called on, the benches on both sides, except that of the front Opposi- tion, were filled, and a small crowd of members occupied the Space below the bar. NOTICES.—The following notices were given :—Mr. Jesse Collings, to move a resolution in favour of free education ; Mr. Kennard, on Wednesday to ask the late Presi- dent of the Board of Trade whether he was correctly repor- ted to have said that the rule of Ireland by the late Govern- ment was unjustifiable oppression, and to have compared it to that of Russia in. Poland, and of Austria in Venice, and if so whether the Cabinet of which he was a member agreed to the course pursued in the tribunal, or in his denunciation of a course pursued by Russia and Austria in Poland and Venice.—Mr. CHAMBERLAIN : I think I can save the time of the House if I answer at once. (Hear, hear, and laugh- ter.) I did not use language which I think is capable of bearing the interpretation pat on it by the hon. member. What I did say was that the Government of Ireland re- sembled that of Russia in Poland, and of Austria in Venice in its centralised and bureaucratic character. (Oh, oh, and hear, hear.)—Mr. Hopwood, that in case a motion should be made in regard to the letter from Mr. Bradlaugh, he would move the following as art amendment :—" That Mr. Brad- laugh, the member for Northampton, having Wormed the Speaker of his intention to come to the table to be sworn, the House is of opinion that the questions raised concerning promissory and other oaths call for settlement on a wider ground than the interest of a particular constituency or its member, and resolves to proceed with legislation on that subject as soon as possible." Prtovistoner. ORDERS.—Mr. CrEo. RUSSELL moved the third reading of the bill to confirm certain provisional orders of the Local Government Board relating to the boroughs of Stafford and Wigan and the local government districts of Ulverston.—The motion was agreed to, and the bill was read a third time and paused. LORD SALISBURY ACCEPTS OFFICE.—STATEMENT BY MR, GLADSTONE. MR. GLADSTONE then rose and said: Information has been conveyed to me enables me to acquaint the House that Lord Salisbury has definetly accepted Office ; that the designation and appointment of his Cabinet are in an ad- vanced stage, so much SO that he ,confidently expects— if it be the pleasure of she House to sit to-morrow—that the new writs may be moved for those seats vacated by the acceptance of office. The course most convenient to take now—l have no doubt the House will be disposed to corn- ply—is that I should move, first, that the Standing Order which relates to Sittings on Wednesday should be sus- pended, and that the House at its rising do adjourn till five to-morrow, that being the hour indicated by Lord Salisbury on the part of the incoming Government. After that I shall move that the House do forthwith adjourn. THE MEDICAL RELIEF BILL dic. Mr. JESSE Commit:4s remarked that an arrangement had been made between the leaders of the two parties to press forward certain bills but he asked for some assaance that the Medical Relief Disqualification Bill shbuld be included among the important measures on whicn they had agreed, otherwise he should take the sense of the House upon the question, and in the absence of an assurance from the Prime Minister he should oppose the adjournment. Mr. Labouchtre wished to know if the Prime Minister would now give the promised atai‘mout iu regard to the negotiations that had taken place with respect to any 4 assurances that might be given to right hon. gentlemen opposite before they assumed office. Mr. GLADSTONE: With regard to the question which has been put to nie—vr-ry naturally and property put—l believe that Lord Salisbury is of the same opinion as myself, that not a moment ought to be lost that Can be taken advantage of in giving to the lieuse the information we think they are entitled to with respect to the recent communications. I have great hope that it will be in my power to give that in- formation to-morrow. I cannot speak positively, as it de- pends on the concurrence of others ; but such is my hope , and clothe. I cannot give any account of the correspon- dence or of the principles that have guided us in our con-

duct, but very soon hon. gentlemen will be able to form their own opinion upon a correct knowledge of everything that has taken place. That is all I think I need say on that particular subject. Then my bon. friend the member for Ipswich (Mr. Collings) asked if is true that an agreement has been made between the leaders of the party which is now coming into office and the leaders of the party that is going out of office with respect to the progress of certain bills, and he says that the arrangement does not include a bill in which he is very much interested, and which cer- tainly has strong claims to be brought under the judgment of the House. I think I can effectually relieve the mind of my hon. friend. There is no foundation whatever for the statsment that such an arrangement has been made. No communications of any kind have taken place on the subject. The promise that I gave t) the House re- mains absolutely unimpaired, and under the circumstances I think the second reading of such a bill ought not to be moved in the absence of a responsible Government. The motion was then agreed to. Mr. GLADSTONE then mewed the adjoutement of the Hoisse.—This motion was also agreed to, and the House adjourned at 4-45. _
HOUSE OF COMMONS.-WEDXESDAY.
There was no sitting in the House of Lords to-day. In the House of Commons the Speaker took the chair at five o'clock.

There was a large attendance of members on both sides. Mr. Gladstone and his colleagues having resigned the seals of office, the Liberals took their seats on the Opposition side of the House, and the Conservatives occupied the Min- isterial Benches. The only occupants of the Treasury bench were Sir Arthur Otway, chairman of committees; Mr. Rowland Winn, Alderman Fowler, and Alderman Cotton. Mr. Gladstone entered the Rouse at five o'clock, and was received with loud cheers from his supporters. TIER New WRITS.—Lord Richard Grosvenor moved for a new writ for Wakefield, in the room of Mr. Mackie, deceased.
LORD SALISBURY'S DEMANDS UPON THE LIBERAL LEADERS.

STATEMENT BY MR. GLADSTONE. Mr. ROWLAND WINN, who.was received with Ministerial cheers. said : I beg to move that the House at its rising do adjourn till Friday, the intention being that no business should be transacted except the issue of certain writs that lam not in a position to issue to night. On Friday I shall propose that the House should adjourn till Monday week, the Oth July.

Mr. GLesosrotex, who was received with loud Opposition cheers, said: Perhaps the motion which has just been made, and which I should have been happy to second if it had been necessary, may afford me a convenient and regular opportunity of fulfilling the pledge which I have given on more than one occasion to the House. It is strictly in con- formity with the pledge given by me to the House in re- spect to questions which have been put to me by the hon. member for Northampton, and I shall now proceed to read, with her Majesty's permission, all the lettsrs containing assurances as to the conduct of my friends and myself which I have given through her Majesty in answer to the request of Lord Salisbury. I shall read those letters without note or comment of any kind, except to say that there is one of them from myself to her Majesty from which one or two sentences have been or will be omitted, as they are sentences that have hardly any bearing upon the real points of the cor- respondence, but relate to matters that may possibly here- after come into discussion. The first letter was one of Lord Salisbury's, dated June 17, 1885, in which his lordship pressed for specific plsdges—first, that Mr. Gladstone and his friends would support a motion to give the new Govern- ment precedence on all days on which financial business is put down, the new Government engaging not to bring for- ward on those days any other business ; secondly, that if no other provision were made by the House for the credits already voted and the estimates laid on the table, Mr. Glad- stone and his friends would support a financial arrangement to the effect that the income tax shall stand for the year at 83, and that in lieu of any other augmentation of taxation provision be made for Supply either by Exchequer bonds for the year or any other form of temporary loan. Lord Salisbury added that as the constitutional resource of an appeal to the constituencies had been cut off by the Redistribution Bill he and his friends could not take office with any ad. vantage unless they received from the leader of the major- ity an engagement to concur in the measures which were indispensable for closing the business of the session.—Mr. GLemsrosm submitted this request to his colleagues, and then pointed out to tier Majesty that it would be contrary to public duty to compromise the liberties of the House of Corrimons by giving the specific pledges which Lord Salis- bury required. In the conduct of the necessary business of the country during the remainder of the session he believed there would be no disposition to embarrass the new Gov- ernment, but he did not consider it would be for the public advantage to enter into specific pledges on points of Par- liamentary action with respect to which he was not in pos- session of all the facts that bear upon them.—ln acknow- ledging the receipt of this letter, Lord SALISBURY stated that he was not able to understand on what ground Mr. Gladstone spoke of the "specific pledges" asked for as compromising the liberties of the House of Commons. The closing letter from Mr. Glad- stone, which is dated June 21st, is as fellows "Mr. Gladstone presents his humble duty to your Majesty. He had the honour to receive, soon after one to-day, your Majesty's gracious letter. He has at no time stated that nothing could be done in the sense indicated by Lord Salis- bury, and has indeed reason to believe Lord Salisbury is already aware that in his opinion facilities for expediting Supply may reasonably be provided, but not so as to place the liberties of the House of Commons in abeyance. But his colleagues have been of opinion that it would not be advisable to enter into argument or detail on the demands of Lord Salisbury, and Mr. Gladstone could not but concur, as his reference to the recent conferences on the Seats Bill has simply led to counter arguments. With regard to fin- ance, looking at all the facts and probabilities before him, Mr Gladstone feels sure there is no idea of withholding the ways and means required for the public service, and he ap- prehends no danger on this score. The difficulty which he Is unable to surmount lies in endeavouring to define before- hand the course to be taken on questions, the exact form of which cannot be foreseen. He remains, therefore, without power on his own part and that of his friends to tender the -specific pledges required by Lord Salisbury." In conclu- sion, Mr. Gladstone said: I have now read, with Her Majesty's permission, all the letters containing assurances as to the conduct of my friends and myself, which I have given through Her Majesty in answer to the requests of Lord Salisbury. (Liberal cheers.) Mr. WINN said that as he was informed the Rouse of Lords would meet to-morrow in accordance with an arrange. meat previously made, he begged to withdraw the motion that the Rouse adjourn until Friday. The motion was withdrawn. On the motion of Mr. Wpm, new writs were issued for North Devon, East Gloucester, South-West Lancashire, Woodstock, Westminster North Lancashire, Launceston, Dublin University, Middlesex, North Leicestershire, Mid- Lincoln, Hertford, and Mid-Kent.—Mr. PARNELL having given notice that he should take an early opportunity of calling attention to the administration of the Crimes Act in Ireland by the late Government, the House adjourned at a quarter to six. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TRunspay.
Their Lordships met at a quarter to tour o'clock, the new Lord Chancellor (Giffard) being on the woolsack, and the Conservatives on the Minister!al benches. _ _

ROYAL ASSENT.—The Royal assent was given by com- mission to the Princess Beatrice Annuity Bill, the Redistri- bution of Seats Bill, the Burial Boards (Contested Election) Bill, and 27 private bills. IRE PRIME MINISTER ON THE RECENT _ _

div.p: CRISIS.

The Marquis of SALISB—IIITYM—ade a statement in refer- ence to the political events of the past few days, and the part he and Mr. Gladstone had taken in them. Upon being summoned to Balmoral he ;nlvised her Majesty that it was desirable under the peculiar circumstances of the case that the Government then in office should take charge of the management of Parliament during the abnormal interval that must elapse before constituencies could ba consulted. The opinion was communicated to Mr. Gladstone, who replied that his Government was pre- cluded from reconsidering its resignation. Pledges were then asked for, and the correspondence read in the other House on Tuesday night followed, the result being that Mr. Gladstone declined to give specific pledges. In the last letter of the correspondence, however, his attitude was somewhat modified, and although his pledges were not specific they were specially inclined. At this stage Her Majesty intervened, and called attention in very earnest language to the injury that was being done to the highest interdsta of the State by the prolongation of the crisis. It was urged by the Queen that he might reasonably accept Mr. Uladstone's assurances. He felt that if he now declined the responsibility of office be should be compelling Her Majesty to recur either to new leaders or to new conabina- tious, that a long delay must necessarily intervene, and that the evils of suspense would probably exceed any evils they might incur by dispensing with Mr. Gladaton's specific assurance. Under these circum- stances, and with the unanimous consent of his colleagues, he thought it was his duty to assume office. He trusted the next four or five weeks would show that they struck the balance in the right direction. The time bad not come when he could make any statement of the policy of the Government, but be hoped to be able to make one in a few days. In the meantime be hoped they should not meet with any large number of politician who would of set purpose and • desire impede the progress of the Government. Some distinguished men talked of the cer- tainty of their being swept off the face of the English con- stituencies from Devonshire to Cheshire. He deprecated prophecies of that kind, and did not think it was their duty to take such probabilities into account in devoting them- Selves to the performance of their duty to their country and their Queen.—Earl GRANVILLE expressed an opinion that no apology was necessary from the noble Marquis for taking office, as be had followed a perfectly constitutional course. Referring to the correspondence, the noble Earl remarked that the course taken by Her Majesty had been with regard to both the outgoing and the incoming Administrations of a perfectly constitutional character. MISCELLANEOUS.—The Friendly Societies Act (1875) Amendment Bill was read a second time. The Yorkshite Registries Bill passed through Committee. The East India Unclaimed Stocks Bill was read a third time and passed.— On the motion of the Marquis of Salisbury, their Lordships adjourned at five o'clock ontil--so far as regards legislative business—Monday, the 6th of July. div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.

LONDON', THURSDAY. The series of surprises by which the Ministerial crisis -has advanced to its natural conclusion have been fully maintained during the past week. A week ago to-day, as the correspondence read by Mr. Gladstone in the House of Commons last night ahowsl Lord Salisbury had suddenly discovered that be could not take office. Some days earlier he had intimated his final resolution to accept the Queen's invitetion, and Parliament stood adjourned till Friday last with the expectation that it would then meet and see the writs issued for the re-election of the new Ministers. Then came this sudden bearing- in upon the mind of Lord Salisbury that unless Mr. Gladstone would undertake to exercise a friendly guardianship over the Ministry that had superseded him it would be impossible for the Conservatives to take office. Two things Lord Salisbury specifically demanded, and they were two, only because there could not by any possibility have been more. He wanted Mr. Gladstone to guarantee that the rights of private members should by wholesale be set aside in favour of the new Government, and that so objection should be offered to a proposal to carry over till next year the deficit created by the re- fusal of the House of Commons to sanction the in- ereaeed duty on spirits, beer, and the death duties. Never since Ministries began was there made such a monstrously cool proposal. It was as if a man had entered your house, turned you out, taken forcible possession, and then invited you to devote your time and energies to keeping 'him in quiet possession and making things comfortable all round. Mr. Gladstone, of course, declined to give the specific assurances demanded, and, as the cor- respondence shows, Lord Salisbury reiterated his statement of the impossibility of his assuming the responsibility of Government unless he had the pledges asked for. Thus on Friday when the house met the air was full of rumours that Mr. Gladstone and his friends were coming back, an impression that grew stronger through Saturday and Sunday., and on Monday morning was every- where received. On Monday night a change came over the situation. Nothing had been definitely said, but in the higheat Liberal circles it was assumed that Lord Salisbury had swallowed his protest, and would take office. At this particular time matters looketl on paper in the most highly strained condition. Mr. Gladstone had reiterated his non posauntur, and Lord Salisbury in his latest letter had, repeated his. But here, in a manner most marvellous, Lord Salisbury's portion in the correspondence ceased. Whilst Mr. Gladstone was seated in Downing-street awaiting formal intima- tion of Lord Salisbury's refusal of office, he /earned that the Conservative chief had definitely accepted the post offered to him, was making appointments right and left, and would on the next day go down to Windsor to confer with the Queen. What happened in the counsels of the Conserva- tive leaders between Wednesday, the 17th of June, and Monday, the te'nd, is a secret at present• well kept. The 'natural assumption is that on the Wed- nesday Lord Salisbury convinced himself of the im- passibility of forming a Ministry out of the per- sonal jealousies of his party, and that at some hour on Monday morning these objections were removed. It is necessary to form a theory of this or some other kind, as it is impossible to suppose that Lord Salisbury would, merely for the fun of the thing, put himself in the ridienlous position of having made certain specific demands upon his political opponent, and at the end of a long correspondence putting his tail between his legs and walking off with an air of really not having been saying or writingeanything. As it is, the Marquis does not escape the bitter reproaches of his own party. They perceive that, at the very outset of a Government hampered in many ways, they have been placed in a ludicrous position without an apparent advantage even having been contemplated. All the comings ind goings, the hopes and fears, the reports and the contradictions, are now happily over. Lord Salisfeary's Ministry is practically com- pleted. Mr. Gladstone sits in the seat of the leader of the Opposition; and on Monday week the glass ceiling of the House of Commons will look down, surely not without astonishment, upon Lord Ran- dolph Churchill seated on the Treasury Bench be- tween Sir R. Cross and Mr. W. H. Smith. In many ways this transformation scene is unique. We have had before, and many times, a change of Ministry; but never a change so oddly brought about, nor a Ministry BO strangely constituted. Above all, never was there an Opposition so jufdlant. Mr. Gladstone has renewed his youth like the eagleeand no one even whispers the word Retirement. The load of the Empire having been taken off his shoulders he once more walks erect, with smiling face, brightened eye, and a cheerfulness of manner which has long been foreign to him. Probably the memorable vote , of the 9th of June saved his life. It has certainly rejuvenated him and furnished him with an op- portunity of preparing for the great November Cam- paign, a consequence probably not in the mind of Sir M. H. Beach when he moved his amendment. The Lord Mayor when he issued invitations for his dinner "To meet Mr. Speaker " at. the Mansion House last night, little thought that on his left hand would sit Sir Harding& Giffard, Lord Chancel- lor, sign of mighty changes in other directions. This incident. RR may be supposed, did not, so far as the Lord Mayor was concerned, mar the fes- tivities. Although the guests were very fairly chosen from both sides of tele Howie, Mr. Fowler, as is well known, is a stout Tory, and rejoices exceed- ingly in the change of ministry. Personally he has an interest in it, as it secures to him that baronetcy which he has so well deserved_ The most remark- able incident in the evening was the reception given to General Lumsden. When his name was read out by the toastmaster in the list of guests to whom the Lord Mayor drank in the loving cup, a burst of cheering followed which lasted several minntes. It was renewed when he rose to respond to the toast of the army. This was of course a demonstration against the late Government, who would not go to war with Russia since they could attain their objects by peaceful means. Sir Peter Lumsden is a tall, rather fine-looking man, a little muddled in his speech. But of course speech mak- ing is not the chief business of a soldier. Visitors to London who chance to arrive by morn- ing trains are apt to be surprised as they near the capital in pausing an outward-bound excursion, from which shrill hurrahs aro poured in plentiful profusion. These ebullitions of feeling proceed from the participaters in one of the many day in the country "trips which are just now in full swing. Sunday school vies with Sunday sehool in the en- deavour to give a day's thorough enjoyment to the children ; and though the enthusiasm which attends the morning hours is not so niarkedly displayed on the return journey, it is only because the pleasures have been so many awl so great that the little ones, are too tired to shout as they come back towards home. That there are abases of the system all who are concerned in it will allow, and not the least is the facility with which children join a Sunday school on purpose for the treat, and flit to another as soon as it is over, so as to stand a chance for a second outing. But the general enjoyment is so great that it would require much more serious drawbacks thao these to cause the public to withhold their support. The flower industry in London seems to grow with each succeeding summer, and the casual visitor cannot hut wonder, when he sees in the morning the main thoroughfares thronged with flower sellers, whether it is possible the whole stock can be cleared before night. There ie exceedingly little that is picturesque among the vendors. The traditional "fair flower is a being to be dreamt of and not seen; but though the sellers are mostly frowsy, and a consider- able proportion look as if they would be the better fdrt wash, their ware.; are always acceptable in a hot and dusty city, and the sale is enormous. , is curious to watch the course of hotel building in London. The Grand surpassed the Charing-cross, and now the Metropole distances the Grand. Lon- don is being gradually, indeed rapidly, Americani- zed. In the West End mansions of six ot seven stories height are planned for flats, while the cen- tral situation.; are devoted to enormous hotels. Just at the top of Haymarket, the west corner of Coven- try-st.. ands Great Windmill-at., there was a kind of hilt public, half eating-house, notable because years ar Miss Nielson was employed there as a barmaid. This house and the three or four adjoining it, west of it, have been pulled down, and they are ,nOW bliiding a splendid pile oti the site of it. It is of Bath stone, and when completed will be rather in the style of the buildings of which the Princess Theatre is Part. The ground floor will be shops. above will he a handsome hotel, while in the centre 'will be the Pavilion Music Hall It is quite a Lon- don sight te rev the workmen employed on this building. Day and night the. work is carried On: fro-hi gangs of men relieving those employed till otni-,et atid working through the night till dawn. the electric light being more brilliant than the sun. At midnight on Saturday there is a lull, but when the clock has struck twelve on Sunday night the Auk week's labour begins. It is expected at this ,

rate that the "music hall will be completed in a 1 couple of months. I have just heard of the very serious illness of \ Mr. Pownoll Williams, one of the most promisimng and original of our landscape painters. I don't thin k he ever exhibited at the R.A., but year after year had his own exhibition in the Haymarket. Hewes out on the river a few days ago and got a sun- stroke. lam told his condition is very critical. At the Lyceum the other evening I saw an in- teresting group in the manager's box. It consisted of several of the French actors, and notably Jane Hading, who seemed fascinated by Ellen Terry. I I hear their visit was not without significance, and that Jane llading intends to have a French version of Olivia produced at the Gymnase. Dame's version of Hamlet is to be brought out at the Francais next winter. It will be strange if "adapted from the English" should become a familiar phrase on French play bills. . .

div.p: 4,.)'ettar to the editor.
"SOMETHING WORTH RRaDLLIO.'

•. Sir,.—! think you will allow with me that the above is a sufficiently striking beading for a letter. It is not original. I have borrowed it from a leaflet that has been put into my hands, as ales into the hands of other workmen, the same leaflet being somewhat of a literary curiosity. After reading the above attractive beading, I read on --"Fu :l employment, fair wages, and happiness, or partial employment, loss in wages, and anxiety. Make your own choice." Now I siy this leaflet begins in such an attractive form that one is led to fear lest it should all turn out a me e "puff " before the end was reached. With me this dread turned into a certainty, for sure enough ere many words were read the Tory's cloven hoof was cleally discernibb., the vote of the working-man was being angled for, the bait being Protection or Reciprocity. No one Can possibly have any objection to a Tory pamphleteer saying that "The drones for a time live upon the honey which the working bees have made.' Radicals have been saying this for years, and know as well as any one that" non-producers grow rich out of the goods made by the producers;" the only point in which we differ is as to who are the 'non-producers." Suppose Ste take Lord Salisbury Or Mr. Gladstone as non-producers, wou'd our anonymous writer therefore deprive them of their posses- sions? No. not with these does he wish to meddle, but with the "merchants who live in the fine houses in out- skirts or suburbs of Liverpool." Now, working-men, I ask you, can you for a moment be led away by so shallow a pretext? Can you for a moment imagine that these Liver- pool merchants will help you in the least to cut off their supplies? You may rest assured that they are Tories, and will watch any Tory Government at a game o( that sort. But our great sin lies in "the work- ing population producing goods at low prices," aided by "great improvements in machinery speeded by steam power." Now all this evil comes about in consequence of the "non-prodricer " stepping in again and be-Taniev the "industrial population " with a "Free Trade policy" whereby they have to produce "ten times more" while at the same time they cannot live "ten times cheaper." Really, ills surprising to what lower depths the Tory mind can descend. Wtiat is implied in my quotations is, that if we had bad prohibitive tariffs at all our seaports, old machinery and old methods of working would have sufficed I to procure to Rngland'a workmen their share of the world'd I trade.

Sir, lam obliged to say that offering this " rot " to the British workman is an insult to his intelligence. It is an insult and a deliberate mystification of words to say that the "non-producer by sending foreign made goods into our colonies still further reduces our wages." To give efTect to this statement, Fair Traders should try to persuade cm colonies to buy in the dearest market, and see what thei.• r-ception would be. America, by ke-ping cheaper goods Oat of her markers, forces her peonle into the hands of mon- opolists, and we see what are the consequences ; wages are reduced, arid strikes are of such magnitude as we in Eng- land happily know nothing of. We are told that the trade with our colonies can be al- _

tered and improved, if we will only vend those persons to Parliament who will give attention to the industry of this country. I have before me a list of the tariffs imposed by our colonies on all imported goods. Boots. shoms, coals, candles, soap, ploughs, machinery, salt, in fact everything is highly taxed, salt paying as much as 22s per tea. Now, I ask is there a working-man sufficiently simple as co think all these taxes would be removed by the absurd expedient of resorting to retaliatory methods. The idea is monstrous. Farther than this, we are told what sort of men we mast send to Parliament. Why, look amongst the business men of Warrington, and where is there one, either Liberal or Conservative, that will pledge himself to support a Protec- tion Government? If there was anything in the cry for Protection are we to suppose that the heads of the large firms in Protection, would take no steps to educate their workmen on the question? If we look in the House of Commons, what do we see is its composition ? The Tory side is made up chiefly of landowners, mm who produce nothing, and yet this sapient writer tells us to beware of 'non-producers;" men who think a great deal more of our said nobility than they think of British c immerce. Lopk on the Liberal benches, and we see men whose incumes are chiefly derived from trade, whos) lives hive been pissed in the counting-house, who hope to pass on successful busi- nesses to their eons. Are these men blind on the question of Fair Trade? Surely not; and this is a strong reason why working-men must be careful not to be gulled by a mere Tory electioneering dodge. we are to take steps to benefit trade, and I think we ought to do so, let us at the coming election support no man who refuses to make the land question the chief plank in his political programme. Remember that from the land we get our ore, we get our coal ; and remena bur also that this ore, and this coal pays a royalty to the" non-producer" which, if the manufacturer bad the benefit of it, would give him such a margin that reduction of wages and strikes would become obsolete terms. I have more than once reminded your readers of the great hindrance to trade caused by the excessive railway charges Remember it WAS railway influence prevented Mr. Chem- berl sin from reforming all this, and that the Chairmen and Board of Directors on all the railways are chiefly Tories, or they are in sue:lent numbers to out-vote anything that would be likely to benefit trade. CLIFFORD DIX.

THE LIBIL(RY.—An adjourned meeting of the trustees was held on Tuesday evening to consider the placing of the library under the altered conditions through the c )11aps. of the Worwing•men's Society. It was considered best to leave the matter in abeyance until two of the trustees. who are from home, the Rev. H. MacNaghten and Mr. W. L. Evans, are able to be present. In the meantime the lihrety remains closed.

A LAZY VAGRANT AT PRESCOT.—At Widnes Petty See- on Wednesday, a man named Alfred Scruton was charged with neglecting to do the required work whilst an inmate of the casual ward of the Prescot union Workhouse. The taskmaster at Whiston Workhouse said that prisoner was admitted to the vagrant ward on the 18th inst., for the second time in the same month. Ha was ordered to pick oakum, and in three days he picked 3ths., insm.d of doing 41bs. each day. He was sent to prison for 14 days. with bard labour.

RELIEF REV:MRS.—Mr. Hall, workhouse -nester, reported that there were 423 inmates in the workhouse this week, against 435 last week, and 394 in the corresponding week last year. There has been 44 vagrants relieved during .tho week. against 51. in the same week last year. A letter dated the 11th June was also read from Messrs. a fly. This Was broußbt to Sidney Smith as a great curiosty, and a remarkable thing to see. He (Sidney Smith) said: " Well, there was not much in the thing itself, the only wonder was how the devil it got there." (Laughter.) He had told them why he was there, and the question was—Why his opponent was where he was. (Renewed laughter.) If it was not yet clear he would make it so. The Tory party in Cheshire— they had all been cone tiering the Northwich division, from Lora Egerton down to that violent, vapouring parson, the ' Rev. Mr. Preston—(loud laughter)—from the top to the bottom of the Tory party they knew there was no chance far that party without a split amongst the Liberals. It was because there appeared to be a chance of a split that they had put up, as a figure-head, Mr. William Henry Verdin. What , From an Egerton to a Verdin. Where were the gal- lant country gentlemen, to stand up, manfully leading their followers as hitherto to victory ? Where were the country gentlemen, the men of long lineage, the men who defended the privileges of the aristrocracy ? (Laughter) Where where the men who had taught them always "God bless the Squire and his relations, and keep us in our proper stations ?" (Laugh- ter.) Did they remember how Sir Charles Dilke quite recently took upon himself the office of prophet, and declared that the Liberals should sweep the counties from Devonshire to Cheshire. He looked to them to disap- point the vain hopes of the Tories, and to procure a very amine and real fulfilment of Sr Charles Dilk's prophecy. (Applause.) Referring to what has taken place in Ministerial affairs, Mr. Brunner said that Mr. Gladstone is as keen, clear, and determined as ever he was to maintain our liberties. (Applause.) Mr. Gladstone had before him a noble programme, and might he be spared to carry it out for our benefit. (Applause,) Mr. Brunner then proceeded to saeak of poli- tics generally.

AFFRAY BETWEEN SOLDIERS AND POLICEMEN AT WARRINGTON. A rather serious affray took place between soldiers and policemen last evening week, the circumstances of which were investigated at the Borough Court on Saturday morning, when four soldiers of the South Lancashire Regiment (Orford barracks) were brought up on charges of a serious nature. Their names and the charges against them were stated as fellows:— Jones Moran, drunk and disorderly, and assaulting P.C. Hardy and P.S. Jones; Thomas Moore, assault- ing P.S. Jones, P.C. Paine, and P.S. Cox; Michael Culeen. a.saulting P.S. Jones, P.O. Hardy, P.C. , Palm, P.S. Cox, and P.C. Monaghan; John Koran, I assaulting P.S. Jones, P.C. Paice, and P.C. Turner. One of the prisoners appeared to have been rather severely punished, and several of the policemen con- cerned had sustained injuries. From a statement made by Chief Constable Hunt, it appeared that P.C. Hardy was on duty near the Theatre Royal on the evening of Friday. Shortly after eleven o'clock he advis A a number of soldiers, who were quarrelling in the streets, to go home, awl thereupon James Moore asked what he had to do with the matter. Prisoner Thomas Moore then pushed Hardy against the wall, a struvgle followed, and the two fell to the ground. James Moran was seen by the constable to take off his belt, and he told the other soldiers to do the same. Constable Paice and Sergeant Jones came no, and a fight which listed five or ten minutes took place. Attempts were made by the soldiers to rescue Hardy's prisoner, and a number of bystan- ders ran to fetch the assistance of other constables. Police Sergeant Cox, who was at Market Gate, was informed of the occurrence, and, as he was going down Horsemarket-street, towards Scotland-road, he met prisoner Moore running towards- him with his' belt in his band. Cox stopped him and, told him that he should want him. Moore went with him quietly for a time and then became violent, but was ultima- tely lodged at the pelice station. James Moran was also secured. Culeen, who was concerned in the affair, was known to the police, and was apprehended at midnight, but, after going quietly for a time, he became rough and escaped. He was, however, fol- Sowed and re-captured by P.C. Monoghan. From in- formation received P.C. Turner went to apprehend John Moran, who, when near the Central Station, sucezeeded in making his escape. He also was recap- tured, but the constable was afterwards seriously as- saulted by him and some women. There were two men still at large. In concluding his statement, Mr. Hunt said that the affair was a sad one to him, as he had hoped that a better feeling had sprung up between the military and the police. He must also say, with regard to Sergeant Jones and P.C. Hardy, that ha had not two better tempered or more forebearing men in the force than they.—PO Hardy, in giving evidence, said that all four prisoners used their belts. Hitl fioger was bit Iby someone, his head was cut in three places, and he was black about the thighs with kicks re,,eived whilst on the pround.—Sergeaut Jones spoke to having his eager bitten, and being severely kicked, and P.C. Pelee to being kicked.--Evidence was also given by P.s. Cox, P.C. Monoghan, P.C. 'Pittner, John Nic- holls, Philip Maguire, and John Hickey, aft-r which the Bench, expressing determination not to tolerate such assaults, sent Culeen to prison for six months with hard labour, and the other three prisoners to the House of Correction for three months with hard labour. Three girls, fustian cotters, named Winifred Con- way, 27, Bank-street, Margaret O'Brien, Town-bill, and Mary Ellen Keeley, Catherine-street, were then charged with being drunk and assaulting PA Cox and P.C.'s Monogban and Turner. The assault was committed while the officers were apprehending one of the soldiers. Conway and O'Brien, who were old offenders, were each sent to prison for a mouth, and Keeley for fourteen days.

div.p: A WARRINGTON LADY AIIATEUR.

Mrs. Green%ll, the wife of Colonel Greenall, of Warrington, made her deiut on the stage on Wednes- day at the Vaudevillef Theatre, London, under the nom de plume of "Miss Angela Fenton." The matinee, under the patronage of the Duke and Duchess of Edinburgh, was well attended, and was in every respect completely successful, A London correspond- ent s sys : —" The Merchant of Venice" was the play chosen, Miss Fenton, of course, taking the part of Portia. Success under such circumstances, with an uncritical and evidently well-disposed audience' can- not mean very much, and may mean vary little, but it must be admi.ted that the new aspirant for dramatic fame made fewer calls than might have expected upon the friendly indulgence of her hearers. She had been carefully, if not very intelligently, trained, and has plenty of nerve and self-possession. Her voice is good— not rich, but clear and pleasant— and her fate, if not endowed with great depth or variety of expres- sion, is piquant and attractive. Her stage bearing is unconstrained, but her attitudes and gestures are, Is yet, monotonous. These, however, are matters whkh further experience and practice will easily amend. On the other hand, she will certainly find it diffi 3ult to attain the breadth of style, the mobility of expres- sion and the dignity of carriage requisite for the heroines of the poetical drama, of whom Portia is, perhaps, the chief. In the casket scene neither her speeches nor her by-play gave adequate expression to the conflicting emotions of the character. She played gracefully, but no more. In the trial scene her cos- turns, though very effective, was a decided innovation. Instead of the long cassock descending to the ankles, which is the traditional dress of the part, she wore a black velvet doublet, black hose, and a watered-silk gown, also of black, but with a crimson lining both to the body and to the flowing sleeves. In this costume her appearance was sufficiently pleasing, bat lacked the grave dignity neceisary to give anything like verisimilitude to the scene. Her delivery of the famous lines on mercy was not ineffective, and altogether her inexperience was in this scene less apparent than might have been expected. On the whole, however, it is probable that if Miss Fenton adheres to the profession of the stage she will find her true calling in modern drama rather than in poe,ical comedy. It must be admitted that she seemed more at home on the stage than several of the professional actors who supported her.

-RUNCORN LIBERAL ASSOCIATION..

A ward•meeting of the voters of the West district of the I North wieh Parliamentary Division, comprising Greenwey- road, Higher Runcorn, Newtown, Percival-lane, and the streets or roads communicating therewith, was held in the Bethesda Schoolroom, Runcorn, last evening, when there was a good attendance. The chair was occupied by Mr. Kniveton, and an address who delivered by Mr. J. T. Brun- ' ner, cand.date for the Nortbwich Division. The Chairman, in introducing Mr. Brunner, congratula- ted the audience uponehe happy citcumstances under which they were met, the Redistribution Bill having received the Royal aseent—(applause)—and now we had a measure that the Liberal party had been working bard to accomplish eyer sluice 1872. He hoped that their meeting together at at various times would result in their not only making the acquaintance of their candidate, but their future member. (Applause.) Mr. Branner, who was leceived with cheers, said that he thought the executive of the Liberal Attsocietion had done wisely in advising him in the first instance to address his constituents in small sections, because on occasions like the present, end in rooms like that, they should become rather better acquainted with each other—they came nearer face to i.ce than they could at very large meetings, whin well- known, possibly illustrious statesmen, would very likely be invittd to address them. He addreesed them, they knew, as their selected candidate, but it was impossible to expect that he was chosen by every house- holder in Runcorn, or that every householder knew him, liked hem, and professed his principles, and therefore , it was thet he wished to meet them, to talk to them, and if ' they pleased, to hear what they had got to say. (Ap- plause.) Bye and by it was hoped tie have large meet- ings in the largest of the town's buildings, and to hear some amongst his friends who lately were high in office, and perhaps, as a friend 1 of his a few months ago suggested, men now of greater freedom and less responsibility, who would come and aid them in the contest for the division. (Applause.) It seemed to him that on that, the first occasion on which he addressed an entirely public audience in Runcorn, he should say why he was their candidate. Why was he there? Well, they knew, the siecessery cause of a man't being any- where was his father's courtship. It was absolutely neces- sary for a man to be anywhere that his father should have gone through the process of courtship. It was a very in- teresting fact to him, though perhaps hardly imerestine to them, that a part of his father's courtship was carried on in Runcorn, so that his connection with Runcorn was rather elder than himself. (Laughter.) His reason for telling that was that he had been called a foreigner—(laughter) an intruder, that it had been widely spread, or an endeavour had been made to spread, the idea widely that they should not vote for anyone who was not born in Cheshire, and had not lived in Cheshire all his life. Well, be was born in sight of Cheshire. and had laved in eieht of Cheshire,. or in Cheshire, ever since. (Ap- plause.) He was an ambitious man, but that was not the reason why he was there. He was perfectly aware before he made up his mind to offer his services that he should be op- posed by a geetlernan—and a friend of his—who would ask for their suffrages. To is man like himself, who had been brought up all his life to feel himself under a great serse of responsibility for his actions, he had great seamhings of heart before he could take up that position. He consulted with men who wore thoroughly familiar with the Liberal cause, and asked them one after another to consider with him the situation in the North- wich whether if a salt manufactuter was chosen many of the new voters, rudely called raw salt boilers, would vote Tory, and for ever after be Tories. If it did turn out that any considerable Dumber of men were led to vote for a salt manufacturer as such, if he were a Tory be granted them that a very serious evit would have been done. He recognised that fact before he became a cendi• date, bet on the other hand he asked his friends, and finally broueht them round—they did not all want ccnyincing— they finally agreed with him upon one point—that the can- didate must he a thorough Liberal—(applause)--or no good would be done. If there had been no contest in the North- wich Division—and that flattering prospect had been held out—did they take it that the raw salt boiler would thereby have been made a Liberal; did they take it that ' H the king of the salt trade bad been chosen as a cendi- date for that divieion because he was that king, and no vote had been given, that that would have mule their, and ehair fellows Liberals. No! And therefore it was not because he was an ambitious man, eut because be was a Liberal—because he was determined to do all that was in his power to procure that the division should be represented by a Liberal—that he asked for their suffrages. (Applause.) He Leek it that that association did not honour him with its choice because he warn an alkali maker. He took it that the association honoured him because of 20 years of CONBI3- tent, bard work, for Liberal principles. (Applause.) Well, and how about his gallant opponent? Ha knew that am a matter of conrtesy,„a gentleman bearing her Majesty': conimistion was at once honourable and gallant. Mr. William Henry Verdin was an officer in her Majesty's ser- vice, and nes his (the /meeker's) gallant opponent. He acknowledged, in the first instance, that Mr. Verdin had bit herto said no word tbat could hurt his feelings, and be ack-noelklged with greater pleasure that he had not tie smallest fear that Mr. Verdin would ever say a word that would pievent him off.tring and receiving the hand of frieretsbip with him. SPECIAL SEEL:HONS.—Oa Sanday two sermons were preached by the Rev. C F. Rogers, orgamizrng secretery for the northern division of England of the National Society for Promoting the Educatien of the Poor in the Principles of the Established Church. The morning sermon was a dis- course on the subject of perfecting the educagon of the people. A strong point urged was that it wee not sufficient to engrave facts on the minds of the children only. There was a requirement beyond that which they must attend to. At the evening service the address was based on "The un- chaogeaole nature of God—the same yesterday, to-day, and for ever." The congregations were good, and the collec- tions, which were in aid of the sniety, amounted to £8 lie WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL ANNIVERSARY —The 82nd anniversary sermons in connection with the Lymm Wes- leyan Sunday Schools, which are the oldest in the village, and are attended by about 140 scholars, were preached on Sunday, morning and evening, by the Rev. George Dickin- ens, of Hebden Bridge. A large number of people from Warrington, Altrincham, and other places in the neighbour- hood were present. Special hymns were sung by the scholars in a highly creditable m Anna, they having received careful training at the hands of Mr. Newburn. In the after- noon the sacred cantata, entitled "Under the Palms: or the Jewish Flower Feast," was rendered by members of the 'choir, Mr. Newburn officiating as conductor. Mr. Edwin I Brown, jun., presided at trio pianoforte, and Mr. F. 0, Moe- ton at tho organ. There was a large attendance, and many were unable to gain admittance, the room being crowded in every part. The sopranos were—Mrs Pearson, Miss E. E. Moston, Miser Bertie Leigh, Miss Hazeldine, and Miss Lizzle ! Joees ; contraltos. Mrs. Chorley and Mies Brown;. tenors, I Messrs. Ferris, H. Holt, Thomas Changer, and J. Rogerson; bawl, Messrs. J. Massey, F. Howard, W. B. Moeton, lir Brown, and W. It dditt. The fellowing also took part in the can- tata—Miss Mary Leigh, Miss Mary Elliott, and Mr. Walter Moston. The choruses were rendered by the scholars and choir, and Mr. G. Brereton gave a recitation in a pleasing mariner. The performance WAS a musical treat,,and gave every satisfection. The colleerions for the day amounted to £2l, which was in excess of the amount collected in pree vious years. On the following day the annual treat to the scholars took place. Assembling at the school at half-past I one, the children were formed into procession, and after- wards walked through the streets•of the village, headed by the superintendent, Mr. E. Brown, sen. At various points on the way they sang several of the anniversary hymns, and ' then marched back to the schoolroom, where they were re- galed with tea. Subsequently the scholars. were taken to a field near the chapel, which had been kiedly lent by Mr. Winetanley. • Here they at once commenced their enjoy- ment—cricket, racing, and other trstimes being engaged in. A libaral supply of nuts and sweeets, which had been con- siderately provided by Mr. Decide, who has recently taken up his residence in Lymm, was distributed, and greatly ap- preciated. Having enjoyed themselves to their hearts' con- tent, the children were dismissed to their homes about niue. o'clock.

DATE OF THE DISSOLUTION.—Witb respect to the question of which Mr. Heneage has given notice, the Daily/Nein is in a position to state that the Government have resolved to , dissolve Parliament immediately after the Seats Bill comes I into operation. The general election will therefore take place about the middle of November. STRIKE AT HODDERSFIELD.—On Friday morning the twiners and piecers employed by six firms of cotton spin- ners hi Hudder,sfield, numbering nearly 300, strthk work I against a proposal made by the masters to reduce their I wages ten per cent. The notice of reduction was given a fortnight ago, and expired on Thursday night. £2 nnn DAMAGES FOR INJURIES —ln the Queen's Bench Division on Friday Mr. Thomas Penny, Chittenden, com- mercial traveller, was awarded by the jury £2,000 damages , for injuries sustained ai Millbay StatL.n, Plymouth, whilst %a passenger on the Great Western Railway. The engine of the train by which the plaintiff was trvelling came into violent contact with the stationary buffers, with the re- result that the plaintiff received injuries to his spine and nervous system. The defendants had admitted their lia- bility.

div.head: SHIP CANAL BILL.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL BILL.

..... On Thursday, the Chairman of the Ship Canal Commit- tee announced that Mr. Dalrymple, one of the members of the cotnmittee, bad accepted office under the Crown, and either a fresh member mast be appointed er the committee must get leave to go on with three members Haying stated the reasons for and ageinst these alternatives, Mr. Forster said be himself thought they should ask for leave to eit with three membe,s, but be invited an expression of the feeling of the several parties concerned. Mr. Pember, for the promotns, agreed in the chairman's view ; and Mr. Popo, for petitioners against the Bill, said his clients had no objection to the proposal. It may be stated that in the House of Commons Committee the Chairman has a casting vote, and, therefore, four members are usuaNy considered equal to five, which is the number generally requisite to form a committee of ihe House of Lords. THE ALTERNATIVE PLAN.

- - At the adjourned inquiry which was held on Fridayl before only three members, Mr. Forster presiding, the chair- man remarked upon the apparent similarity between the plan proposed by the promoters and that put forward last veer as an alternative plan by Mr. Lyster, engineer to the Mersey Dock Board, and. he ask.d the promoters whether if It were thought desirable they could adopt Mr. Lyster's Pember having anticipated the question read a statement of the views of the promoters, the effect of the statement being that while they might accept Mr. Lyster's plan laterally and alter the course of the canal so as to in- fringe as little as possible on the estuary, they could not alter the level to that of Mr. Lyster's plan. Ile added that he saw no reason why the dredging powers proposed to taken under clause 29 should not be limited to one or two Points, as for instance opposite the entrance to Ellesmere Port, aed in that case the fears of the opponents that a new channel would be produced along the Cheshire shore must disappear.

The weekly meeting of the Provisional Committee was held in the Boardroom, Manchester, on Friday afternoon, Mr. Henry Boddington, junior, presiding. The reports from the Parliamentary Committee in London, as to the progress of the bill were received with much interest, and the deter- mination of the Select Committee to prevent all needless repetition of evidence was highly approved as conducive to the interests of both promoters sad opponents. It was felt that substantial progress had been made since the last meet- ing. After the usual routine business had been got through the committee adjourned. _

div.head: TWE NEW GOVERNMENT.
div.p: TWE NEW GOVERNMENT.

FIRST CABI;;;;:ME;;ING—.-1:The'fit-inee-ting of the new Cabinet was held at noon on Friday at the official residence of the First Lord of the Treasury in Downing-street. A group of spectators bad assembled to watch their arrival. Sir Michael Beach was the first to arrive, having been pre- viously engaged for some time in the transaction of official duties as Chancellor of the Exchequer. The Duke of Richmond was next, followed by Mr. (*lbsen, the new Lord Chancellor of Ireland. 'Lord John Manners then drove up, after which Viscoent Cranbrook walked across from St. James's Park. The Marquis of Salisbury arrived in his brougham, and was cheered by the assembled crowd. He acknowledged the greeting by raising his hat, Sir Richard Cross walked up with the new Lord aancellor. At the same time the Earl of Crrnarvon, Lord Randolph Churchill, and Mr. W. H. Smith arrived, followed shortly afterwards by Lord George Hamilton, the Earl of HarrewbV. and Colonel Stanley. The council broke up at half-past one. The Duke of Richmond.was the brat to leave, and a • , few minutes later Lord Harrowby, Lord John Manners, Lord George Hamilton, and Mr. Smith, left in company for the Foreign Office, where they were speedily joined by Lord Salisbury and Lord Randolph Churchill, who walked together. It is stated Viet the Council was summoned for the purpose of considering chiefly the financial situation, and of deciding upon the policy to be followed in connection therewith. PART! LEADERS IN COMIUNICATION.—The Central News learns that active comnffinications have been passing be- tween the Liberal whips and the leading Members of the Government during the last few days. On Friday morning Sir William Harcourt, Lord Kensington, and Lord Richard Grosvenor had a long consultation. CONSERVATIVE POLICY De THE SOUDAN —A telegram from Alexandra, on Friday, says Lord Salisbury ins sent a telegram to Lord Wolseley, sympathising with his views en evacuation, but declaring his inability, for various reasons, to maintain the expedition to the Soudan. THE "CopS DIPLOMATIQUR" RECEIVED BY LORD SALMI/ORE.—The Marquis of Salisbury, Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs, held an official reception of the Corps Diplornatique on Friday afternoon at the Foreign Office. Count Munster, German Arnbass tdor ; Count Nigra, Italian Ambassador; Musurus Pacha, Turkish Ambassa- seder ; and M. de Staal, Russian Ambassador, were pre- sent. .

BARON, DB WORMS.—The Press Association is informed that Baron de Worms, M.P., has been offered and has ac- cepted the post of Parliamentary Secretary to the Board of Trade. Be has appointed Mr. W. D. Lawrence as his pri- vate secretary. Mn. GLADSTONE.—Mr. Gladstone called in Downing- street on Friday morning at half-past ten o'clock, having walked over from Richmond•terrace. The rigbt hon. gentleman carried a email black bag, and was accompanied bra friend. Mr. Gladstone remained in Downing-street until near noon, when he left just before the new ministers began to assemble for the Cabinet Council.

div.head: DEPRESSION IN TUNIS.
div.p: DEPRESSION IN TUNIS.

Borax. FRlDAY.—lntelligence received from Tunis states that a French popular meeting was held hers on the 21st Inst., in the theatre, with the object of considering the causes of the present commercial and financial crisis in Timis. The great majority of those present attributed the fault to M. Cambon, the French Minister resident. After numerous speeches had been delivered, it was decided to ask for M. Cambon's recall, and a long telegram was sent to Faris to that effect. The proceedings passed off quietly. A few Italians, Belgians, and Germans attended. Another meeting is expected to be held en the 27th inst. TEIE SEIZURE OF_ENCiLISIi FISHING, SMACKS.

BERLIN, FRlDAY.—Jadgmmt has been given by the tribunal at Aurich in the Case of Dosset and Wright. mas- ters of the two English fishing smacks, recently taarn at Wilhemshaven by the German despatch boat Pomerania, on the charge of fishing in prohibited waters. The accused were condemned to six weeks' imprisonment, inclusive of the time during which they were detained in custody, and to the payment of the costs of the legal proceedings. The court also ordered the confiscation of their fishing appara- tus. The public protpcutor had demanded that the prisoners should he condemeed to two months' imprisonment.

SERMONS—The Rixton Wesleyan Sunday School sermons were preached on Sunday, afternoon and evening, by Mr. F. Ward, of Altrincham, to large congregations. Th. sing. log was conducted by the Cadishead Sa.red Tonic Sal-Fa Class, under the management of Mr. W. L, Brown. Me rendering of the anthems and hymns gave very great sati3- fac.ion. There were good collections.

A SCANDAWIIS MISIIAP.—On Saturday a funeral was ap- pointed to take place at half-past four eclock in the even- ing in the Cadishead Burial Ground. The ministert, how- , ever, on reaching the place found the family grave full, the List coffin being within the number of foot of the surface describod by law. The Sexton on being required to give an ' explanation, said the fault was no his, as be told the pit. ties concerned ; hut they on the other hand said it was not so. The minister was thus plated in circumstances of per- plexity. Had he consented to bury another in the same grave be would have been liable to a fine as well as the family of the bereaved. There was no time to dig another grays the same evening. Hs was therefore obliged to meet the funeral party on the way and, explain matters. Next day (Sunday) the young man was buried at 1114141 in l4(l' Parish Church-yard.
